open_questions/0.rationale: The eosinophil model is coherent and is directly evidenced in hypereosinophilic syndrome, where the acute infiltrative stage, the thrombotic stage, and the fibrotic stage are all observed prospectively in the same patients. In tropical endomyocardial fibrosis, none of that is observed. Patients present at the fibrotic stage, eosinophilia is usually absent by then, and biopsy at that point is uninformative in a specific and vicious way, because degranulation and replacement by fibrosis erase the evidence of the very process being looked for. The inference therefore runs backwards from a shared end-stage appearance, which is exactly the reasoning pattern that would also be satisfied if two different upstream processes converged on one scar. The alternative worth taking seriously is that the endemic disease is driven by something else entirely, with the eosinophilic endocarditis of hypereosinophilic syndrome being a separate route to the same architecture. Population screening now makes the decisive study possible for the first time, because it identifies affected people before the fibrotic stage.

evidence.snippet: Despite several hypotheses regarding cause, no account of the etiology of this disease has yet fully explained its unique geographical distribution.
evidence.explanation: The systematic review's conclusion, which is the premise of this gap.

open_questions/1.rationale: This is the constraint every etiologic hypothesis has failed. Filariasis and schistosomiasis are widespread far beyond the endemic zone; cassava is eaten across the tropics; malaria's distribution does not match the disease's. A systematic review across six decades concluded that no proposed account explains the geography. Three structurally different explanations remain open. The cause may be a genuinely localised exposure not yet identified, such as a soil geochemical factor, in which case the geography is the signal rather than the puzzle. It may require a specific conjunction of exposures that happens to co-occur only in those regions, in which case single-factor studies were always going to fail. Or the apparent geography may be substantially an artefact of where anyone has looked, which population screening in non-endemic tropical regions could test directly and cheaply.

evidence.snippet: Most affected subjects had mild-to-moderate structural and functional echocardiographic abnormalities. Only 48 persons with endomyocardial fibrosis (22.7%) were symptomatic.
evidence.explanation: The observation that creates the question, with the numbers that make its resolution consequential.

evidence.snippet: By using echocardiography, we were able to detect early, asymptomatic stages of the disease.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own interpretation, that these are early stages, which is the reading the proposed follow-up would test.

open_questions/2.rationale: Screening a rural Mozambican population found echocardiographic disease in nearly a fifth of people, but only 22.7 percent of those were symptomatic and most had only mild-to-moderate abnormalities. Two readings have opposite consequences. If most screen-detected cases progress, then the clinical disease is the visible fraction of a very large iceberg, screening would identify a huge population for early intervention, and the prevalence figure is a public-health emergency. If most are stable, then the screening criteria are detecting a common structural variant or a self-limited healed lesion, and treating the prevalence as a burden estimate overstates it substantially. No longitudinal follow-up of a screen-detected cohort has been published, so the question is open on the evidence rather than merely contested.

evidence.snippet: These immune markers seem to be related with activity and might provide an adjunct tool for diagnosis and classification of EMF, therefore improving its management by identifying patients who may benefit from immunosuppressive therapy.
evidence.explanation: States the activity correlation and the therapeutic hope that rests on the causal reading.

evidence.snippet: it is unclear whether the primary target of injury is the endocardial endothelium, the subendocardial fibroblast, the coronary microcirculation or the myocyte
evidence.explanation: The authors' framing of the unresolved question about what is being injured, which this discussion extends to what is doing the injuring.

evidence.snippet: There was no statistically significant difference in the overall risk of developing grade 3 ascites over 8 weeks.
evidence.explanation: The one attempt at immunosuppression in this disease, and it was negative on its primary endpoint, which constrains the therapeutic argument this discussion turns on.

open_questions/3.rationale: Anti-myocardial IgG is present in about half of patients and a tenth of controls, and its intensity correlates with disease activity. Correlation with activity is compatible with both readings, since an antibody that drives injury and an antibody that reports injury would both track it. The authors of the only study explicitly declined to resolve it. The stakes are concrete rather than academic: only the causal reading would justify trialling immunosuppression in a disease that currently has no medical therapy at all, and giving immunosuppression on the strength of a marker would expose a malnourished, often parasitised population to real harm. That trial has in fact been attempted once. A pilot randomised trial of prednisolone in 35 Ugandan patients found the drug safe but failed to show a reduction in ascites reaccumulation, with a relative risk of 0.70 and a confidence interval crossing one. It targeted the ascites rather than the autoantibody arm, and with 16 patients on active drug and six lost to follow-up it cannot exclude a modest effect, so it does not settle this question. It does mean the question is no longer purely hypothetical, and that any future immunosuppression proposal has to say what it would do differently.

evidence.snippet: The volume of publications on endomyocardial fibrosis has declined since the 1980s.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the decline in research attention to a disease of this prevalence.

evidence.snippet: can be used to expose global disparities in cardiovascular research
evidence.explanation: The authors' own framing of the disease as an index of research inequity.

open_questions/4.rationale: This entry has no transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, or single-cell data to cite. It has exactly one molecular-profiling study of any kind, a plasma cytokine panel in 27 patients, and one randomised trial, a 35-patient pilot of prednisolone that was negative. Its only genetic association has never been replicated, its only animal model dates from 1996, and the only cell system in use is explicitly described by its own authors as not a disease model. That is the entire modern molecular literature for a disease affecting nearly a fifth of a screened population. Publication volume has fallen since the 1980s. These are not properties of the biology; they are properties of where the biology happens. The curation consequence is that absence of evidence in this entry should not be read as evidence of absence anywhere it appears, and that flagging a gap here is frequently a statement about research funding rather than about a hard scientific problem. This is recorded as a standing caveat over the whole entry rather than as a question with an experiment attached.

evidence.snippet: At least 22 genes are associated with Fanconi anemia, constituting the Fanconi anemia DNA repair pathway.
evidence.explanation: Core complex genes form the upstream signaling arm of the FA pathway.

steps/22.description: Mutations in FA core complex genes (FANCA, FANCB, FANCC, FANCE, FANCF, FANCG, FANCL, FANCM, UBE2T/FANCT) disrupt the E3 ubiquitin ligase that monoubiquitinates the FANCD2-FANCI complex, abolishing the central signaling step of the FA pathway. FANCA mutations account for 60-70% of all FA cases.

evidence.snippet: proteostasis deregulation itself is driven by excess sterile inflammatory activity in hematopoietic and stromal cells within the fetal liver, and dampened Type I interferon signaling similarly restores fetal Fancd2-/- long-term hematopoietic stem cells to wild type-equivalent numbers.
evidence.explanation: Inflammatory signaling in the BM microenvironment drives HSC loss in FA.

steps/23.description: Excess sterile inflammatory signaling (TNF-alpha, interferon-gamma, Type I interferons) in the bone marrow creates a hostile microenvironment for HSCs. Both hematopoietic and stromal cells contribute to chronic inflammation, driving proteostasis deregulation and accelerating stem cell attrition.

evidence.snippet: In addition to overexpression of p53 and TGF-β pathway genes, we identified high levels of MYC expression. We correspondingly observed coexistence of distinct HSPC subpopulations expressing high levels of TP53 or MYC in FA bone marrow (BM).
evidence.explanation: scRNA-seq of primary FA patient HSPCs identifies MYC as a novel driver of BMF alongside known p53/TGF-beta pathways.

evidence.snippet: Inhibiting MYC expression with the BET bromodomain inhibitor (+)-JQ1 reduced the clonogenic potential of FA patient HSPCs but rescued physiological and genotoxic stress in HSPCs from FA mice, showing that MYC promotes proliferation while increasing DNA damage.
evidence.explanation: BET inhibitor targeting MYC rescues genotoxic stress in FA mouse HSPCs, validating MYC as a therapeutic target.

steps/24.description: Single-cell RNA sequencing of primary FA patient bone marrow HSPCs revealed MYC overexpression as a novel pathogenic driver alongside p53 and TGF-beta upregulation. Distinct HSPC subpopulations co-expressing high TP53 or high MYC coexist in FA bone marrow. MYC-high HSPCs show downregulation of cell adhesion genes (including CXCR4), promoting enhanced egress from bone marrow to peripheral blood and contributing to HSC exhaustion and bone marrow failure.

evidence.snippet: reprogramming transcription during hematopoietic differentiation results in an overload of genotoxic stress, which causes aborted differentiation and depletion of FA mutant progenitor cells. DNA damage onset most likely arises from formaldehyde, an obligate by-product of oxidative protein demethylation during transcription regulation.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that transcriptional reprogramming during differentiation generates formaldehyde-induced DNA damage that specifically depletes FA-deficient progenitors.

steps/25.description: Transcriptional reprogramming during hematopoietic differentiation generates a surge of genotoxic stress from formaldehyde, an obligate by-product of oxidative protein demethylation during transcription regulation. In the absence of functional FA DNA repair, this differentiation-associated DNA damage causes aborted differentiation and depletion of FA progenitor cells, providing a mechanistic explanation for the hematopoietic-specific failure in FA despite it being a germline disorder.

evidence.snippet: FANCA-deficient human HPCs underwent accelerated terminal differentiation driven by activation of p53/p21. We identified growth arrest specific 6 (GAS6) as a novel target of activated p53 in FANCA-deficient HPCs and modulate GAS6 signaling to rescue hematopoiesis in FANCA-deficient cells.
evidence.explanation: iPSC-derived FA model reveals p53/p21/GAS6 axis driving progenitor exhaustion and validates GAS6 as a therapeutic target.

evidence.snippet: disease model iPSCs displayed drastically defective cell expansion when stimulated into hematopoietic differentiation in vitro, displaying increased levels of DNA damage. The expansion defect was partially reversed by treatment with a new small molecule termed C1, which is an agonist of ALDH2
evidence.explanation: ADH5/ALDH2-deficient iPSCs modeling FA-like aldehyde toxicity confirm hematopoietic differentiation defects and identify ALDH2 agonism as a rescue strategy.

steps/26.description: Induced pluripotent stem cell modeling of FA hematopoietic differentiation revealed that FANCA-deficient human hematopoietic progenitor cells undergo accelerated terminal differentiation driven by p53/p21 activation. GAS6 (growth arrest specific 6) was identified as a novel p53 target gene; GAS6 signaling modulation rescues hematopoiesis. This iPSC-based new approach methodology overcomes the lack of faithful murine FA models and enables drug screening for FA therapeutics.

evidence.snippet: Establishing the interaction network involving the FA proteins and their associated partners has revealed an intersection of FA with several DNA repair pathways, including homologous recombination, DNA mismatch repair, nucleotide excision repair, and translesion DNA synthesis.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that the FA pathway intersects with translesion DNA synthesis, establishing the mechanistic link.

steps/27.description: Impaired ability to bypass DNA lesions during replication through translesion synthesis polymerases, requiring functional FANCD2-FANCI complex and PCNA monoubiquitination.

evidence.snippet: We examined 64 Japanese FA patients, and found that the ALDH2 variant is associated with accelerated progression of BMF
evidence.explanation: Human clinical data showing that impaired aldehyde detoxification (ALDH2 variant) accelerates bone marrow failure in FA patients.

evidence.snippet: recent studies have shown a major involvement of the FA pathway in the tolerance of reactive aldehydes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the FA pathway is required for tolerance of aldehyde-induced DNA damage.

steps/28.description: Endogenous aldehydes (acetaldehyde and formaldehyde) from normal metabolism generate DNA interstrand crosslinks and DNA-protein crosslinks; impaired detoxification by ALDH2 and ADH5 exacerbates DNA damage burden.

evidence.snippet: This reflects the indispensable role of FANCB protein in the enzymatic activation of FANCD2 monoubiquitination, an essential step in the repair of DNA interstrand crosslinks.
evidence.explanation: FANCD2 monoubiquitination is the essential central step in ICL repair.

steps/29.description: Mutations in FANCD2 or FANCI disrupt the central ID2 complex whose monoubiquitination is the critical signaling event in FA pathway activation. In wild type, the core complex E3 ligase monoubiquitinates both FANCD2 and FANCI, causing the ID2 heterodimer to clamp onto chromatin at stalled replication forks and recruit downstream nucleases and HR effectors. Loss of either subunit abolishes this signaling hub.

evidence.snippet: At least 22 genes are associated with Fanconi anemia, constituting the Fanconi anemia DNA repair pathway. This pathway coordinates multiple processes and proteins to facilitate the repair of DNA adducts including interstrand crosslinks (ICLs)

steps/30.description: Mutations in FA genes impair the body's ability to repair DNA damage, leading to increased sensitivity to crosslinking agents and propensity for chromosomal instability.

evidence.snippet: the fact that 5 FA genes are in fact familial breast cancer genes and FA gene mutations are found frequently in sporadic cancers suggest wider applicability in hematopoiesis and oncology.
evidence.explanation: Downstream FA genes overlap with breast cancer susceptibility genes.

steps/31.description: Mutations in downstream effector genes (BRCA2/FANCD1, PALB2/FANCN, BRCA1/FANCS, RAD51C/FANCO, XRCC2/FANCU) impair homologous recombination and translesion synthesis. These overlap with familial breast/ovarian cancer genes; biallelic mutations produce the most severe FA phenotypes with early-onset solid tumors and more congenital anomalies.

evidence.snippet: the fact that 5 FA genes are in fact familial breast cancer genes and FA gene mutations are found frequently in sporadic cancers suggest wider applicability in hematopoiesis and oncology.
evidence.explanation: The overlap of FA genes with breast cancer genes (BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2) establishes the connection between FA and homologous recombination repair.

steps/32.description: Defective repair of DNA double-strand breaks following interstrand crosslink unhooking, due to mutations in FA genes involved in HR pathway including BRCA2, PALB2, and BRCA1.

evidence.snippet: ICLs can interfere with DNA transactions, including replication and transcription. If not properly removed and repaired, ICLs cause DNA breaks and lead to genomic instability, a hallmark of cancer.

steps/33.description: Increased tendency for genomic alterations including chromosomal breaks, deletions, and rearrangements.

evidence.snippet: proteostasis deregulation itself is driven by excess sterile inflammatory activity in hematopoietic and stromal cells within the fetal liver, and dampened Type I interferon signaling similarly restores fetal Fancd2-/- long-term hematopoietic stem cells to wild type-equivalent numbers.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that inflammatory signaling drives HSC pool deficits in FA, and that dampening inflammation rescues HSC numbers.

evidence.snippet: the FA proteins might counteract aldehyde-induced genotoxicity in hematopoietic stem cells
evidence.explanation: Establishes that aldehydes cause genotoxicity in HSCs and FA proteins normally protect against this damage.

steps/34.description: Progressive depletion of long-term hematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow due to replication stress, aldehyde-induced DNA damage, and chronic inflammatory signaling.

evidence.snippet: 30% developed myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), leukemia and/or solid tumors
evidence.explanation: 30% malignancy rate reflects ongoing clonal evolution in FA HSCs.

evidence.snippet: Half the patients developed chromosome 1q gain, driving clonal hematopoiesis through MDM4 trisomy downmodulating p53 signaling later followed by secondary acute myeloid lukemia genomic alterations.
evidence.explanation: Longitudinal study of 335 FA patients showing chromosome 1q gain (containing MDM4) as the most common early clonal event, dampening p53 and driving clonal hematopoiesis.

evidence.snippet: single-cell sequencing analyses further demonstrated a polyclonal pattern was present at either MDS or AML stages
evidence.explanation: Single-cell DNA sequencing of FA patients transforming to MDS/AML revealed polyclonal patterns with sequential acquisition of UBASH3A, SF3B1, RUNX1, and IDH2 mutations.

evidence.snippet: we performed multiplexed gene editing of mutational hotspots in MDS-associated genes in human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) followed by hematopoietic differentiation. We observed aberrant self-renewal and impaired differentiation of HSPCs with enrichment of RUNX1 insertions and deletions (indels)
evidence.explanation: iPSC-based modeling demonstrates that RUNX1 mutations blunt the G1/S cell cycle checkpoint in FA, promoting transformation.

steps/35.description: Progressive accumulation of somatic mutations and chromosomal aberrations in genomically unstable hematopoietic cells drives clonal selection and malignant transformation. Characteristic cytogenetic changes include gain of 1q and 3q and loss of 7q. Clones with selective growth advantage expand, leading to MDS and AML. Single-cell DNA sequencing has revealed polyclonal evolution at the MDS stage, with sequential acquisition of driver mutations and MDM4-mediated p53 dampening via chromosome 1q gain as the canonical initiating event.

evidence.snippet: we identify increased protein synthesis rates in the fetal hematopoietic stem cell pool at the onset of hematopoietic failure in Fanconi Anemia, a prototypical DNA repair disorder that manifests with bone marrow failure.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that bone marrow failure is a defining manifestation of Fanconi anemia, with origins in fetal HSC dysfunction.

steps/36.description: Inability of the bone marrow to produce sufficient blood cells due to hematopoietic stem cell defects.

evidence.snippet: The incidence of central nervous system (CNS) abnormalities in FA is higher than previously reported, with a midline predominance that points to impact in the early stages of CNS development.
evidence.explanation: Midline predominance of anomalies supports developmental progenitor loss during embryogenesis.

evidence.snippet: In response to replicative stress and unresolved DNA damage, p53 is hyperactivated in FA cells and triggers a late p21(Cdkn1a)-dependent G0/G1 cell-cycle arrest.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the FA p53 response in patient-derived progenitors is a p21-dependent cell-cycle arrest rather than apoptosis alone; the finding is in hematopoietic cells and is applied to developmental progenitors by inference.

evidence.snippet: Our results show that the acetaldehyde-catabolising enzyme Aldh2 is essential for the development of Fancd2(-/-) embryos.
evidence.explanation: Links endogenous aldehyde genotoxicity to embryonic development in an FA mouse model, supporting aldehyde-driven progenitor loss as a developmental mechanism.

evidence.snippet: p53 was preferentially recruited to the promoters of p21 (CDKN1A) and GADD45a, two genes involved in G0/G1 cell-cycle arrest, but not of BAX, a gene controlling apoptosis, in agreement with low level of apoptosis in these EBV-immortalized cells
evidence.explanation: In FA patient cells the p53 response is transcriptionally biased toward arrest genes over BAX, which is why the node names arrest ahead of apoptosis.

evidence.snippet: murine Fancd2-/- bone marrow LSK cells exhibited a high rate of binucleated cells and apoptosis, a hallmark of cytokinesis failure
evidence.explanation: Apoptosis remains a documented, p53-dependent branch of the response in FA progenitors in vivo, so it is retained in the node rather than replaced by arrest.

evidence.snippet: In in vitro studies, FA cells presented hallmarks defining senescent cells, including p53-p21 axis activation, altered telomere length, mitochondrial dysfunction, chromatin alterations, and a pro-inflammatory status.
evidence.explanation: Review-level synthesis that the FA p53-p21 response produces senescence hallmarks, supporting proliferation arrest as a principal effector alongside apoptosis.

steps/37.description: Unrepaired DNA damage in rapidly dividing embryonic progenitor cells hyperactivates p53 during critical developmental windows, driving p21-dependent G0/G1 arrest and loss of proliferative capacity with apoptosis as one branch of the response. This progenitor depletion underlies the congenital malformations of FA, explaining the midline predominance of anomalies and the correlation between pathway position and congenital abnormality burden. The arrest-versus-apoptosis balance is demonstrated in FA hematopoietic progenitors only; it has not been measured in FA embryonic progenitors, and the field-specific step that selects the radial ray, kidney, ear and heart is recorded as an open hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: Endocrine abnormalities were present in 73%, including short stature and/or GH deficiency (51%), hypothyroidism (37%), midline brain abnormalities (17%)
evidence.explanation: Giri et al. documents 73% endocrine abnormality prevalence.

evidence.snippet: Abnormalities were identified in 18 (90%) patients with FA, the commonest being a small pituitary (68%, p < 0.01 females and p < 0.001 males)
evidence.explanation: Small pituitary in 68% provides anatomical basis for endocrine dysfunction.

steps/38.description: Widespread endocrine abnormalities affect approximately 73-80% of FA patients. Developmental pituitary/hypothalamic defects (68% have small pituitary on MRI), direct effects of genomic instability on endocrine cell function, and chronic illness contribute. Manifests as GH deficiency, hypothyroidism, glucose dysregulation, and hypogonadism. Obesity, dyslipidemia, and metabolic syndrome are also reported in endocrine surveys; those associations do not establish a causal route from gland dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: Abnormalities were identified in 18 (90%) patients with FA, the commonest being a small pituitary (68%, p < 0.01 females and p < 0.001 males)

evidence.snippet: Posterior fossa abnormalities were seen in six cases (30%, p = 0.01) including Chiari I malformation (n = 3), Dandy-Walker variant (n = 2) and cerebellar atrophy (n = 2).
evidence.explanation: Posterior fossa and corpus callosum anomalies reflect early CNS developmental impact.

steps/39.description: Midline brain structural defects from neural progenitor loss during early CNS development. Includes small pituitary (68%), posterior fossa abnormalities (30% including Chiari I malformation and Dandy-Walker variant), and corpus callosum structural variation (30%).

evidence.snippet: Human papilloma virus (HPV) vaccination to reduce the risk for gynecologic cancer in females
evidence.explanation: HPV vaccination recommendation implies HPV is a significant co-factor for epithelial cancer in FA.

steps/40.description: Human papillomavirus infection compounds epithelial cancer risk in FA patients. HPV oncoproteins E6 and E7 degrade p53 and Rb tumor suppressors, further disabling the already compromised DNA damage response. HPV vaccination is recommended to reduce gynecologic and oropharyngeal cancer risk.

evidence.snippet: Solid tumors – particularly of the head and neck, skin, and genitourinary tract – are more common in individuals with FA.
evidence.explanation: Confirms epithelial tissue susceptibility to malignancy in FA.

evidence.snippet: We developed the Fanconi Anemia Cancer Cell Line Resource (FA-CCLR) to foster new work on the origins, treatment and prevention of FA-associated carcinomas. The FA-CCLR consists of Fanconi-isogenic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) cell line pairs generated from five individuals with FA-associated HNSCC, and five individuals with sporadic HNSCC.
evidence.explanation: Isogenic FA/sporadic HNSCC cell line pairs provide a platform to identify FA-dependent cancer phenotypes and test therapeutic strategies.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with FA are hundreds to thousands fold more likely to develop head and neck (HNSCC), oesophageal and anogenital squamous cell carcinomas
evidence.explanation: Computational genomic analysis defined the primary structural variant signature of FA pathway deficiency in squamous cancers, enabling computational classification of FA-associated vs sporadic carcinomas.

steps/41.description: Impaired genome maintenance in epithelial tissues renders them vulnerable to accumulation of oncogenic mutations. Squamous epithelia of the head/neck, oral cavity, esophagus, and anogenital regions are particularly susceptible due to high proliferative turnover and exposure to environmental mutagens including HPV.

evidence.explanation: Demonstrates significantly earlier cancer onset in non-FANCA complementation groups.

steps/138.description: Patients with biallelic FANCD1/BRCA2 mutations have a uniquely severe cancer predisposition with early-onset solid tumors in childhood, including medulloblastoma, Wilms tumor, and neuroblastoma, distinct from the typical FA tumor spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Gingival examination revealed that 9 (35%) children had gingivitis and the other 17 (65%) had normal gingival health status.
evidence.explanation: Cross-sectional oral examination of 26 children with Fanconi anemia found gingivitis in 35%.

steps/185.description: Gingival inflammation is common in children with Fanconi anemia, compounded by poor oral hygiene, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. Oral inflammation is clinically important because it coexists with the lifelong risk of oral squamous cell carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: Oral features of Fanconi's anemia may include increased susceptibility to periodontitis.
evidence.explanation: Case report concluding that Fanconi anemia confers increased periodontitis susceptibility.

evidence.snippet: This study investigated the oral health status of 15 children with Fanconi's anemia, including oral lesions, gingival and periodontal status, and dental abnormalities. All children in the group were found to have a tendency to develop tooth decay and were in need of dental treatment. Two had aggressive periodontitis.
evidence.explanation: Two of 15 children with Fanconi anemia in an oral health survey had aggressive periodontitis.

evidence.snippet: A diagnosis of severe generalized periodontitis associated with systemic disease was made.
evidence.explanation: Independent case report of severe generalized periodontitis in an adolescent with Fanconi anemia.

steps/186.description: Increased susceptibility to periodontitis, frequently aggressive and generalized, reflecting impaired host defense (neutropenia, defective oxygen-radical detoxification) superimposed on periodontal infection.

evidence.snippet: Most erupted teeth showed severe gingival inflammation with some gingival overgrowth and various degrees of periodontal attachment loss.
evidence.explanation: Periodontal examination of a child with Fanconi anemia documented gingival overgrowth alongside severe gingival inflammation.

steps/187.description: Gingival enlargement accompanying the severe gingival inflammation and periodontal attachment loss described in Fanconi anemia.

evidence.snippet: the most common congenital dental abnormalities were: (1) microdontia (44%); (2) congenitally missing teeth (26%); (3) transposition (9%); and (4) supernumerary teeth (4%)
evidence.explanation: Radiographic survey of 26 children with Fanconi anemia identified microdontia in 44%.

steps/188.description: Generalized microdontia is the most common congenital dental abnormality detected on radiographic evaluation in children with Fanconi anemia.

evidence.snippet: the most common congenital dental abnormalities were: (1) microdontia (44%); (2) congenitally missing teeth (26%); (3) transposition (9%); and (4) supernumerary teeth (4%)
evidence.explanation: Congenitally missing teeth were found in 26% of children with Fanconi anemia on radiographic survey.

evidence.snippet: In one patient supernumerary teeth were found, while in another teeth were congenitally missing.
evidence.explanation: Independent oral health study of children with Fanconi anemia also documented congenitally missing teeth.

steps/189.description: Congenitally missing teeth (hypodontia) are a recurrent developmental dental finding in Fanconi anemia.

evidence.snippet: the most common congenital dental abnormalities were: (1) microdontia (44%); (2) congenitally missing teeth (26%); (3) transposition (9%); and (4) supernumerary teeth (4%)
evidence.explanation: Dental transposition, a positional anomaly of the dentition, was present in 9% of children with Fanconi anemia.

steps/190.description: Dental transposition and other positional anomalies of the dentition observed on radiographic evaluation in Fanconi anemia.

evidence.snippet: We describe oral aphthous ulcerations in two siblings with FA.
evidence.explanation: Case report of recurrent aphthous oral ulceration in two siblings with Fanconi anemia.

steps/191.description: Recurrent aphthous oral ulceration in Fanconi anemia, reported to improve with correction of anemia, implicating cytopenia in its pathogenesis.

evidence.snippet: we expand the FA phenotype to include early onset osteopenia/osteoporosis and lipid abnormalities
evidence.explanation: The NCI Inherited Bone Marrow Failure Syndrome study explicitly expands the Fanconi anemia phenotype to include early-onset osteopenia and osteoporosis.

steps/192.description: Frank osteoporosis arising unusually early, established as part of the FA endocrine phenotype rather than solely a consequence of transplantation. This is the osteoporosis end of the spectrum captured jointly by the `Osteopenia and Osteoporosis` phenotype in this entry, curated separately so the distinct HPO term is queryable.

evidence.snippet: insulin resistance in 41.7% (10 of 24)
evidence.explanation: Systematic endocrine profiling of 24 patients homozygous for a FANCG founder variant found insulin resistance in 41.7%.

evidence.snippet: abnormal glucose/insulin metabolism (39%); obesity (27%); dyslipidemia (55%); and metabolic syndrome (21%)
evidence.explanation: Abnormal glucose/insulin metabolism was documented in 39% of the NCI Fanconi anemia cohort, alongside obesity, dyslipidemia and metabolic syndrome.

steps/193.description: Insulin resistance is a common component of the metabolic endocrinopathy of Fanconi anemia and can be present before any transplant exposure.

evidence.snippet: Absolute numbers of B cells and natural killer (NK) cells were reduced compared to controls
evidence.explanation: Cross-sectional immunological assessment of children with Fanconi anemia found reduced absolute B and NK cell numbers relative to controls.

evidence.snippet: Among FA patients, a decreased proportion of T CD8(+) and NK CD56(dim)CD16(+) cells were observed when compared to healthy controls
evidence.explanation: An independent cohort of 42 patients with Fanconi anemia confirmed reduced cytotoxic T and NK cell subsets.

evidence.snippet: this is the first report showing a defective degranulation mechanism leading to abnormal NK-cell cytotoxicity in FA-patients
evidence.explanation: Identifies a defined NK degranulation lesion behind the reduced cytotoxicity, supporting an intrinsic NK defect rather than a simple numeric deficit.

evidence.snippet: We performed a detailed immunologic assessment in a large FA cohort who have not undergone bone marrow transplantation or developed malignancies.
evidence.explanation: The cohort design excludes transplantation and malignancy, establishing that the NK and B cell abnormalities are not transplant consequences.

steps/194.description: Quantitative and functional immune defects in Fanconi anemia independent of transplantation, with reduced NK and B cell numbers, reduced NK perforin/granzyme content and impaired NK and cytotoxic T cell function.

evidence.snippet: Bone marrow biopsy revealed hypoplastic marrow, peripheral blood smear revealed pancytopenia, and chromosomal breakage testing was also positive.
evidence.explanation: Marrow biopsy in a child with Fanconi anemia demonstrated a hypoplastic (hypocellular) marrow.

steps/195.description: Hypoplastic, hypocellular bone marrow underlies the progressive pancytopenia of Fanconi anemia and is the histological correlate of marrow failure.

evidence.snippet: Patients with FA often present with bleeding and infection, which are symptoms related to thrombocytopenia and neutropenia.
evidence.explanation: Neutropenia is described as a characteristic cytopenia underlying the infectious presentation of Fanconi anemia.

steps/196.description: Reduced absolute neutrophil count as part of progressive marrow failure; together with thrombocytopenia it produces the classic presenting combination of infection and bleeding.

evidence.snippet: Patients with FA often present with bleeding and infection, which are symptoms related to thrombocytopenia and neutropenia.
evidence.explanation: Infection is a common presenting problem in Fanconi anemia, related to neutropenia.

evidence.snippet: death was due to bleeding in 44.7%, infection in 34%, leukemia progression in 16.0% and graft versus host disease in 5.3%
evidence.explanation: In a 175-patient single-centre Fanconi anemia cohort, infection accounted for 34% of deaths.

steps/197.description: Susceptibility to infection in Fanconi anemia arises both from neutropenia secondary to marrow failure and from intrinsic defects of the NK-cell and B-cell compartments demonstrable independently of transplantation. Infection is one of the two leading causes of death.

evidence.snippet: The first patient presented with epistaxis, petechiae, ecchymosis, and lower limb edema.
evidence.explanation: Petechiae were among the presenting features in a genetically confirmed case of Fanconi anemia.

steps/198.description: Petechial rash as a presenting manifestation of thrombocytopenia in Fanconi anemia.

evidence.snippet: The first patient presented with epistaxis, petechiae, ecchymosis, and lower limb edema.
evidence.explanation: Ecchymoses were a presenting feature in a genetically confirmed case of Fanconi anemia.

evidence.snippet: The first clinical symptom was thrombocytopenia in 83.4% of patients.
evidence.explanation: Thrombocytopenia, the substrate for easy bruising and mucocutaneous bleeding, was the first clinical symptom in 83.4% of a 175-patient Fanconi anemia cohort.

steps/199.description: Easy bruising and ecchymoses secondary to thrombocytopenia, often the earliest clinical sign of marrow failure.

evidence.snippet: increased chromosome breakage and radial forms on cytogenetic testing of lymphocytes with diepoxybutane (DEB) and mitomycin C (MMC)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states that the diagnosis of Fanconi anemia is established by increased chromosome breakage and radial forms after DEB and MMC exposure.

evidence.snippet: diagnosis based on a profound sensitivity to DNA-crosslinking agents can be used to identify the pre-anemia patient
evidence.explanation: The diepoxybutane analysis protocol describes profound crosslinker sensitivity as the basis for cellular diagnosis, detectable even before anemia develops.

steps/200.description: Profound hypersensitivity of Fanconi anemia cells to DNA interstrand crosslinking agents, manifesting as increased chromosome breakage and radial forms after exposure to diepoxybutane (DEB) or mitomycin C (MMC). This is the diagnostic cellular phenotype of the disease.

evidence.snippet: The main role of FA proteins is in the repair of DNA interstrand crosslinks (ICLs).
evidence.explanation: FA proteins function in interstrand crosslink repair; pathogenic variants therefore produce a DNA repair defect and genomic instability.

steps/201.description: Defective repair of DNA interstrand crosslinks by the FA/BRCA pathway is the primary molecular lesion of Fanconi anemia and the cause of its genomic instability.

evidence.snippet: Patients with FA have a high rate of complications from radiotherapy.
evidence.explanation: International Fanconi Anemia Registry cohort receiving postoperative radiotherapy for head and neck cancer had a high rate of severe radiation complications, demonstrating clinical radiosensitivity.

steps/202.description: Clinical radiosensitivity in Fanconi anemia, with a high rate of severe complications from therapeutic radiotherapy. This constrains cancer treatment and is a practical reason for early diagnosis before any oncologic exposure.

evidence.snippet: The incidence of acute myeloid leukemia is 13% by age 50 years.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews reports a 13% cumulative incidence of acute myeloid leukemia by age 50 in Fanconi anemia.

evidence.snippet: Of these neoplasms, 120 (60%) were hematologic and 79 (40%) were nonhematologic.
evidence.explanation: In 754 International Fanconi Anemia Registry subjects, hematologic neoplasms accounted for the majority of malignancies.

steps/203.description: Acute myeloid leukemia is the characteristic hematologic malignancy of Fanconi anemia, typically arising from clonal evolution of the failing marrow.

evidence.snippet: we identified 30 patients with at least one NMSC, either squamous or basal cell carcinoma, or benign tumor
evidence.explanation: Review of 200 patients with Fanconi anemia in the NCI Inherited Bone Marrow Failure Syndrome study identified basal cell carcinoma among the non-melanoma skin cancers observed.

steps/204.description: Non-melanoma skin cancer, including basal cell carcinoma, occurs at markedly younger ages in Fanconi anemia than in the general population and motivates six- to twelve-monthly dermatologic surveillance.

evidence.snippet: A total of 8.6% of patients had leukoplakia or erythroplakia and 3.8% developed malignancy.
evidence.explanation: Retrospective cohort of 105 patients with Fanconi anemia found premalignant oral mucosal lesions in 8.6%, presenting at a mean age of 14.6 years.

steps/205.description: Potentially malignant oral mucosal lesions precede invasive carcinoma in Fanconi anemia and are the target of the recommended six-monthly oral examinations beginning in the first decade.

evidence.snippet: The most common site of primary cancer was the oral cavity (26 of 35, 74%).
evidence.explanation: Of 35 International Fanconi Anemia Registry patients who developed head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, 74% had oral cavity primaries.

evidence.snippet: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma was the most frequent cancer, followed by hematologic neoplasms.
evidence.explanation: In 193 Italian Registry patients, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma was the most frequent malignancy.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of focal somatic copy-number alteration (sCNA) in 55 independent FA SCCs revealed an elevated sCNA frequency relative to HPV-negative sporadic HNSCCs
evidence.explanation: Primary tumor genomics of 55 FA squamous cell carcinomas shows the copy-number-driven signature that distinguishes FA HNSCC from HPV-negative sporadic disease.

evidence.snippet: FA HNSCCs are mostly human papillomavirus (HPV)-negative and frequently carry somatic copy number variations (CNVs), which amplify oncogenes implicated in sporadic HNSCC, but single-nucleotide variants or small insertions and deletions are less frequent than in HPV-negative sporadic HNSCC.
evidence.explanation: Review-level synthesis of the human tumor genomics establishing that FA HNSCC is predominantly HPV-negative with a copy-number-high, low point-mutation profile.

steps/206.description: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma is the most frequent solid tumor of Fanconi anemia and arises predominantly in the oral cavity and oropharynx, decades earlier than in the general population.

evidence.snippet: for complementation group D1 (FANCD1), the bone marrow failure is not a typical feature, but early-onset leukemia and specific solid tumors, most often medulloblastoma and Wilms tumor, are typical for this complementation group
evidence.explanation: Medulloblastoma is described as one of the two characteristic solid tumors of the FANCD1/BRCA2 complementation group.

steps/207.description: Medulloblastoma is one of the characteristic early-onset embryonal tumors of the biallelic BRCA2 (FANCD1) subtype, which presents with childhood malignancy rather than with marrow failure.

evidence.snippet: for complementation group D1 (FANCD1), the bone marrow failure is not a typical feature, but early-onset leukemia and specific solid tumors, most often medulloblastoma and Wilms tumor, are typical for this complementation group
evidence.explanation: Wilms tumor is described as one of the two characteristic solid tumors of the FANCD1/BRCA2 complementation group.

steps/208.description: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is the other characteristic early-onset embryonal tumor of the biallelic BRCA2 (FANCD1) subtype.

evidence.snippet: we report bilaterally hypoplastic scapula with unilateral winging associated with scoliosis and rib abnormality, a previously unreported skeletal abnormality in Fanconi anemia patients
evidence.explanation: Case report documenting rib abnormality together with scapular hypoplasia and scoliosis in Fanconi anemia.

steps/209.description: Costal anomalies occurring as part of the axial skeletal involvement of Fanconi anemia, distinct from the classic radial ray defects.

evidence.snippet: Herein, we report bilaterally hypoplastic scapula with unilateral winging associated with scoliosis and rib abnormality, a previously unreported skeletal abnormality in Fanconi anemia patients.
evidence.explanation: Case report of bilaterally hypoplastic scapulae with unilateral winging in a patient with Fanconi anemia.

steps/210.description: Hypoplasia of the scapulae with winging, an under-recognized shoulder-girdle anomaly in Fanconi anemia occurring alongside scoliosis and rib abnormality.

evidence.snippet: Congenital abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract are not infrequent in FA with renal ectopia being one of them.
evidence.explanation: Renal ectopia is described as one of the congenital kidney and urinary tract anomalies of Fanconi anemia.

steps/211.description: Renal ectopia, including pelvic kidney, among the congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract seen in Fanconi anemia.

evidence.snippet: Eight of these children (20%) with a transfusional iron overload had been undergoing deferasirox treatment during the study period.
evidence.explanation: 20% of 39 children with Fanconi aplastic anemia at a single centre had transfusional iron overload requiring chelation (mean pretreatment ferritin 3377 ng/mL).

steps/212.description: Iron overload from chronic red cell transfusion support for Fanconi aplastic anemia, requiring chelation. This is a consequence of transfusion therapy rather than an intrinsic feature of the disease.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of moyamoya disease (MMD) was suggested by magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) which demonstrated severe stenosis in the right internal carotid artery along with collateral vessel formation in the right basal ganglia.
evidence.explanation: A 9-year-old boy with Fanconi anemia presented with abrupt hemiplegia and dysarthria and had angiographically confirmed moyamoya disease.

evidence.snippet: The association of moyamoya disease with FA is uncommon, and is rarely reported in the literature.
evidence.explanation: Independent case of a 10-year-old with Fanconi anemia and angiographic moyamoya; the authors characterise the association as uncommon and rarely reported.

steps/213.description: Progressive stenosis or occlusion of the terminal internal carotid arteries with collateral moyamoya vessels, an uncommon and rarely reported cerebrovascular association of Fanconi anemia presenting with stroke.

evidence.snippet: supplemental feeding as needed by nasogastric tube or gastrostomy
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists supplemental tube feeding among the standard management measures for Fanconi anemia, indicating clinically significant feeding difficulty.

steps/214.description: Poor feeding and inadequate oral intake are common enough in Fanconi anemia that supplemental nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding is part of standard management, and growth, feeding and nutrition are assessed at every childhood visit.

evidence.snippet: HP:0001824 | Weight loss | Occasional (29-5%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists this as an occasional phenotype in Fanconi anemia.

steps/215.description: Weight loss, an occasional constitutional finding in Fanconi anemia.

evidence.snippet: This study demonstrates the broad spectrum of radial ray anomalies within the FA phenotype along with the possibility of either unilateral or bilateral upper limb differences
evidence.explanation: Analysis of hand differences in 48 NCI Fanconi anemia patients characterised the radial ray anomaly spectrum; 28 had an upper limb difference, always including thumb hypoplasia.

steps/216.description: The upper limb difference of Fanconi anemia spans the full radial ray spectrum, from isolated thumb hypoplasia through radial dysplasia, and may be unilateral or bilateral. Curated as the spectrum-level term alongside the specific `Radial Ray Defects` (radial hypoplasia) phenotype in this entry. Any radial ray anomaly should prompt consideration of Fanconi anemia.

evidence.snippet: including varying combinations and severities of thumb hypoplasia, radial dysplasia and thumb duplication
evidence.explanation: Thumb duplication (preaxial polydactyly) was among the congenital hand differences observed in the NCI Fanconi anemia hand cohort.

steps/217.description: Preaxial (thumb) duplication occurs within the radial ray spectrum of Fanconi anemia, alongside the more familiar thumb hypoplasia and aplasia.

evidence.snippet: due to the presence of atypical findings such as cleft lip and palate, holoprosencephaly, growth restriction and overlapping fingers
evidence.explanation: Case report of prenatally diagnosed FANCO/RAD51C Fanconi anemia with lobar holoprosencephaly, expanding the phenotypic spectrum; the authors describe it as a rare, atypical finding.

steps/218.description: Lobar holoprosencephaly, a rare midline brain malformation reported in FANCO/RAD51C Fanconi anemia and detected antenatally.

evidence.snippet: About 80% of children and adults with FA have at least one endocrine abnormality, including short stature, GH deficiency, abnormal glucose or insulin metabolism, dyslipidemia, hypothyroidism, pubertal delay, hypogonadism, or impaired fertility.
evidence.explanation: Supports the biochemical node. The consensus review recommends growth-axis screening and lists GH deficiency among the endocrine abnormalities affecting about 80% of patients; GH deficiency is established on stimulated GH testing, so this implies a reduced measured concentration without the source stating a level directly.

evidence.snippet: Endocrine abnormalities were present in 73%, including short stature and/or GH deficiency (51%), hypothyroidism (37%), midline brain abnormalities (17%)
evidence.explanation: Supports the biochemical node. GH deficiency in 51% of the NCI Fanconi anemia cohort was established by GH-axis testing; the paper reports the diagnostic category rather than circulating GH values, so this is indirect support for the measured-concentration term and the clinical phenotype is curated separately as `Growth Hormone Deficiency`.

steps/219.description: Biochemical growth-hormone insufficiency on growth-axis testing, one of the commonest endocrine abnormalities of Fanconi anemia and the laboratory correlate of the clinical `Growth Hormone Deficiency` phenotype in this entry. Routine growth-axis screening is recommended.

evidence.snippet: Eighty-two percent of patients had small palpebral fissures, 69% of patients had simple microphthalmia, 64% of patients had small OCD, 55% of patients had microcornea, 28% of patients had ptosis, and 6% of patients had epicanthal folds.
evidence.explanation: Complete ophthalmic evaluation of 22 patients with Fanconi anemia in the NCI inherited bone marrow failure syndrome cohort found microcornea in 55%.

evidence.snippet: Microcornea was present in 18 of 18 eyes, short axial lengths in six of six eyes, steep corneal curvatures in four of six eyes, ptosis in 14 of 16 eyes, short palpebral fissures in 15 of 16 eyes and hypotelorism in three of seven patients.
evidence.explanation: Independent ophthalmological series confirms microcornea in every examined eye of patients with Fanconi anemia.

steps/220.description: Reduced corneal diameter, part of the small-eye ("E" of PHENOS) anthropometric phenotype of Fanconi anemia.

evidence.snippet: Other findings included hypopigmented macules, skin-fold freckle-like macules, extensive sun-exposed freckling, and both hypopigmented and hyperpigmented pigment macules.
evidence.explanation: Full-body skin examination of patients with Fanconi anemia documented skin-fold freckle-like macules and extensive sun-exposed freckling; at least one pigmentary alteration was present in 96.8% of patients.

steps/221.description: Skin-fold freckle-like macules and extensive sun-exposed freckling form part of the characteristic pigmentary morphology of Fanconi anemia, alongside café-au-lait and hypopigmented macules.

edges/23.description: The FA pathway defect itself constitutes the clinically ascertained abnormality of DNA repair

edges/24.description: Failure to repair interstrand crosslinks yields the diagnostic chromosome breakage and radial forms on DEB/MMC testing

edges/25.description: Impaired repair of DNA damage underlies the excess clinical toxicity of radiotherapy in FA patients

edges/34.description: Bleeding manifestations are mediated by thrombocytopenia from the failing marrow

edges/37.description: Gingival and periodontal inflammation in FA is aggravated by neutropenia and impaired mucosal immunity

edges/38.description: Recurrent aphthous-like oral ulceration accompanies neutropenia and cytopenic episodes

edges/39.description: Chronic red-cell transfusion support for marrow failure leads to iron loading

edges/40.description: Unrepaired genomic damage in HSCs triggers checkpoint-mediated apoptosis and senescence

edges/41.description: Genomic instability in embryonic progenitors activates p53-mediated cell death

edges/42.description: Accumulation of somatic mutations drives malignant transformation

edges/43.description: Impaired genome maintenance in epithelial tissues promotes carcinogenesis

edges/48.description: Biallelic FANCD1/BRCA2 loss of homologous recombination function confers early-onset embryonal tumors including Wilms tumor

edges/51.description: Absence of functional ID2 complex prevents recruitment of downstream repair effectors

edges/52.description: Loss of BRCA2/PALB2/BRCA1/RAD51C directly impairs HR-mediated DNA repair

edges/53.description: Chronic inflammatory signaling drives proteostasis deregulation and HSC depletion

edges/54.description: Loss of mesodermal and endodermal progenitors causes organ malformations

edges/57.description: Melanocyte progenitor defects cause pigmentary anomalies

edges/67.description: HPV oncoproteins synergize with FA pathway deficiency to accelerate carcinogenesis

evidence.snippet: Treatment of hypogonadism and GHD is beneficial for bone mineralization.
evidence.explanation: The FA endocrine consensus review supports an endocrine contribution to bone mineralization through the benefit of treating hypogonadism and GH deficiency; it does not make endocrine dysfunction the sole cause of osteoporosis. This is the PMC full text of PMID:25575015, which this entry cites eight times elsewhere; the url form is used because the sentence quoted here is in the body rather than the abstract-only cache.

edges/86.description: Hypogonadism and growth hormone deficiency contribute through impaired bone mineralization; treatment and transplant exposures can also affect bone health.

edges/190.description: Moyamoya arteriopathy is reported alongside FA congenital vascular anomalies but its developmental mechanism is not established

edges/191.description: Refractive error secondary to ocular developmental anomalies such as microphthalmia and microcornea

edges/192.description: Reduced vision follows structural ocular anomalies including microphthalmia, microcornea, and cataract

edges/193.description: Sensory nystagmus can follow early-onset visual impairment from ocular malformations

edges/194.description: Chronic kidney disease develops from congenital renal hypodysplasia and urinary tract anomalies

edges/195.description: Structural urinary tract anomalies predispose to urinary stasis and recurrent infection

edges/196.description: Severe fetal renal malformations reduce fetal urine output, presenting prenatally as oligohydramnios

edges/197.description: The functional counterpart of the structural brain findings this node carries.

edges/198.description: Curated separately from developmental delay because the two are different claims — delay is about the trajectory, disability about the endpoint — and no cited source apportions between the midline malformations, the microcephaly and general ill health as causes of either.

edges/199.description: Cranial nerve involvement, reported alongside the midline and posterior fossa defects this node carries. Whether it reflects a primary neural developmental defect or compression from an associated structural lesion is not resolved in the cited reports.

edges/200.description: An upper motor neuron sign, drawn from this node as the only CNS parent available. One of the weaker attributions in this entry: no cited source localises the lesion.

edges/207.description: Lobar holoprosencephaly is reported in a single antenatally diagnosed FANCO/RAD51C case as part of the midline CNS malformation spectrum; no other FA genotype is cited for it here

edges/208.description: The remaining pigmentary finding, alongside the café-au-lait spots, hypopigmented patches and hyperpigmentation this node already carries.

edges/213.description: MYC overexpression drives proliferation and DNA damage, accelerating HSC exhaustion

edges/215.description: Differentiation-coupled DNA damage depletes progenitors, contributing to HSC pool exhaustion

edges/219.description: Chronic red cell transfusion support for the aplastic anemia delivers the iron load; the overload is a treatment consequence rather than an intrinsic disease feature.

edges/220.description: Platelet deficiency from marrow failure produces the petechial bleeding of Fanconi anemia.

edges/221.description: Platelet deficiency from marrow failure produces easy bruising.

edges/222.description: Adiposity-driven insulin resistance in the adult metabolic-syndrome cluster of the NCI cohort; distinct from the beta-cell secretory defect measured in children, where HOMA-IR was normal.

edges/223.description: Dyslipidemia co-segregates with obesity and metabolic syndrome in the NCI cohort.

edges/224.description: Gingival enlargement accompanying the severe inflammation and attachment loss. The link is indirect rather than direct: the source reports co-occurrence ("with some gingival overgrowth") rather than a causal relation, and ciclosporin — a recognised cause of gingival overgrowth, used in this population around transplantation — is a competing cause that nothing cited distinguishes from the periodontal route.

edges/225.description: Neutropenia from progressive marrow failure is one of the two routes to infection susceptibility; the intrinsic NK and B cell defects are the other.

edges/226.description: Potentially malignant oral lesions precede invasive carcinoma and are the target of the six-monthly oral surveillance.

edges/227.description: Inadequate oral intake is the route to the constitutional weight loss recorded in this disease, and is the reason supplemental nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding is part of standard management. Typed DIRECT on physiological grounds rather than on a sourced assertion: no cited source states the relation in Fanconi anemia specifically, and it is close to tautological outside it.
