genes/22.notes: Aldehyde dehydrogenase 2; detoxifies acetaldehyde. ALDH2*2 variant accelerates bone marrow failure progression in FA patients.

evidence.snippet: a synthetic lethal interaction in avian cells between ADH5, encoding the main formaldehyde-detoxifying enzyme, and the Fanconi anemia (FA) DNA-repair pathway
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that ADH5 formaldehyde catabolism is essential in FA-deficient cells.

genes/23.notes: Alcohol dehydrogenase 5; detoxifies formaldehyde, providing tier-1 protection against aldehyde-induced DNA damage.

evidence.snippet: KMT2D loss decreases the expression of Fanconi Anemia (FA)/BRCA pathway genes under glycolytic inhibition.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that KMT2D loss epigenetically silences FA/BRCA pathway genes under glycolytic inhibition in HNSCC models, the mechanism referenced in this note.

genes/24.notes: Histone methyltransferase; loss in squamous cell carcinomas can epigenetically suppress FA/BRCA gene expression under metabolic stress.

evidence.snippet: hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is the only curative therapy for the hematologic manifestations of FA

treatments/0.description: The only curative treatment for the hematologic manifestations of FA, using reduced-intensity conditioning regimens due to patient sensitivity to chemotherapy and radiation.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Allogeneic HSCT replaces defective FA hematopoietic stem cells with donor cells carrying intact FA pathway function, restoring normal multilineage hematopoiesis.

treatments/0/targets/1.description: Donor stem cells with functional FA pathway resist progressive genotoxic attrition, replacing the depleted autologous HSC pool.

evidence.snippet: Administration of oral androgens (e.g., oxymetholone) improves blood counts (red cell and platelets) in approximately 50% of individuals with FA

treatments/1.description: Can stimulate erythropoiesis and improve blood counts, often used as a bridge to transplantation.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Androgens stimulate residual hematopoietic progenitors to increase erythrocyte and platelet production, partially compensating for the progressive loss of hematopoietic output from FA stem cell attrition.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of growth deficiency, limb anomalies, ocular anomalies, renal malformations, genital anomalies, hypothyroidism, cardiac anomalies, and dermatologic manifestations as recommended by the subspecialty care provider.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends treatment of growth deficiency as part of comprehensive FA management.

treatments/2.description: May be used to improve growth in affected children with short stature.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Growth hormone supplementation corrects GH deficiency arising from pituitary dysfunction in FA, promoting somatic growth in affected children.

evidence.snippet: granulocyte colony-stimulating factor improves the neutrophil count in some individuals
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms use of growth factors as part of supportive care for cytopenias.

treatments/3.description: Treatment of cytopenias with transfusions, antibiotics, and monitoring for malignancy.

evidence.snippet: oral examinations for tumors every six months beginning at age nine to ten years; annual nasolaryngoscopy beginning at age ten years
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends regular oral and nasolaryngoscopic surveillance for early cancer detection.

treatments/4.description: Regular screenings for early detection of cancers, particularly acute myeloid leukemia and squamous cell carcinomas of the head and neck, oral cavity, and anogenital regions.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Regular surveillance detects squamous cell carcinomas and AML-related clonal evolution at early, treatable stages, modulating the clinical impact of FA-driven epithelial cancer susceptibility.

evidence.snippet: Carrier testing for at-risk relatives (for autosomal recessive and X-linked FA) and prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are possible if the pathogenic variant(s) in the family are known.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms the importance of genetic counseling for carrier testing and prenatal diagnosis.

treatments/5.description: Counseling for patients and families regarding inheritance patterns, recurrence risks, carrier testing, and prenatal diagnosis options.

evidence.snippet: gene therapy reverts the transcriptional signature of FA HSPC, which then resemble the transcriptional program of healthy donor HSPC
evidence.explanation: Single-cell RNA-seq of gene therapy-treated FA patients demonstrates molecular rescue of the FA HSPC transcriptional program.

evidence.snippet: a down-regulated expression of TGF-β and p21, typically up-regulated in FA HSPC, and upregulation of DNA damage response and telomere maintenance pathways
evidence.explanation: Gene therapy corrects specific molecular defects in FA HSPCs as confirmed by scRNA-seq.

treatments/6.description: Ex vivo lentiviral-mediated gene correction of autologous CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells with a FANCA-expressing vector, followed by reinfusion without conditioning. Single-cell RNA sequencing of gene therapy-treated patients demonstrates that corrected HSPCs revert the FA transcriptional signature, including downregulation of TGF-beta and p21 and upregulation of DNA damage response and telomere maintenance pathways.

treatments/6/targets/0.description: Lentiviral delivery of functional FANCA restores the FA core ubiquitin ligase complex (FANCA-FANCB-FANCC-...-FANCL) required for FANCD2 monoubiquitination, repairing the DNA crosslink repair pathway.

evidence.snippet: optimizing adenine base editor construct, vector type, guide RNA format, and delivery conditions leads to very effective genetic modification in multiple FA patient backgrounds
evidence.explanation: ABE8e base editing achieves effective correction across multiple FANCA mutation backgrounds.

evidence.snippet: Optimized base editing restored FANCA expression, molecular function of the FA pathway, and phenotypic resistance to crosslinking agents
evidence.explanation: Base editing restores functional FA pathway activity in patient-derived HSPCs.

treatments/7.description: Precision base editing approach using optimized adenine base editors (ABE8e) to correct prevalent FANCA point mutations in patient hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells without relying on double-strand breaks or homology-directed repair, which are impaired in FA cells. Restores FANCA expression and FA pathway function.

treatments/7/targets/0.description: Base editing precisely corrects pathogenic FANCA point mutations at the DNA level, restoring functional FANCA protein and recovering FA pathway capacity for interstrand crosslink repair.

evidence.snippet: Abnormalities in glucose metabolism are frequent in young FA patients without prior diagnosis of diabetes, and are associated with marked defects in insulin secretion.
evidence.explanation: Seed reference; the childhood OGTT study localizes the defect to insulin secretion rather than sensitivity.

evidence.snippet: Insulin and glucokinase mRNA expression were also decreased in FANCC‑depleted 1.1B4 cells.
evidence.explanation: FANCC knockdown in the human 1.1B4 beta-cell line reduced insulin and glucokinase transcripts, giving cell-autonomous in-vitro support for a beta-cell secretory defect; the study models FANCC and oxidative stress rather than first-phase secretion itself.

hypotheses/0.description: Loss of Fanconi anemia pathway function in pancreatic beta cells causes an intrinsic early-phase (first-phase) insulin secretory defect, through unrepaired endogenous DNA damage, p53 activation, oxidative stress and reduced beta-cell mass or function, that is present in childhood before any insulin resistance and independently of transplantation. This would explain why the insulinogenic index is reduced in FA children with normal glucose tolerance while HOMA-IR is unchanged, and why glucose abnormalities progress to diabetes in adults.

evidence.snippet: This study demonstrates the broad spectrum of radial ray anomalies within the FA phenotype along with the possibility of either unilateral or bilateral upper limb differences
evidence.explanation: Seed reference establishing the radial ray spectrum the hypothesis must explain.

evidence.snippet: Our results show that the acetaldehyde-catabolising enzyme Aldh2 is essential for the development of Fancd2(-/-) embryos.
evidence.explanation: Supports the aldehyde-load component of the developmental mechanism in an FA mouse model.

hypotheses/1.description: The radial ray predominance of FA limb malformations reflects a specific vulnerability of the anterior (preaxial) limb-bud progenitor field, where high proliferative demand during the narrow window of radius and thumb specification, combined with endogenous aldehyde load and p53-dependent apoptosis of FA-deficient progenitors, selectively depletes the cells that form the radius, first metacarpal and thumb. Competing explanations include disruption of the SHH/FGF/BMP patterning network rather than progenitor loss, and a shared developmental route with TAR and Holt-Oram syndromes.

evidence.snippet: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma was the most frequent cancer, followed by hematologic neoplasms.
evidence.explanation: Seed reference establishing HNSCC as the dominant solid tumor the hypothesis must explain.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of focal somatic copy-number alteration (sCNA) in 55 independent FA SCCs revealed an elevated sCNA frequency relative to HPV-negative sporadic HNSCCs
evidence.explanation: Primary tumor genomics of 55 FA squamous cell carcinomas shows the copy-number-driven signature that distinguishes FA HNSCC from HPV-negative sporadic disease.

evidence.snippet: FA HNSCCs are mostly human papillomavirus (HPV)-negative and frequently carry somatic copy number variations (CNVs), which amplify oncogenes implicated in sporadic HNSCC, but single-nucleotide variants or small insertions and deletions are less frequent than in HPV-negative sporadic HNSCC.
evidence.explanation: Review-level synthesis of the human tumor genomics establishing that FA HNSCC is predominantly HPV-negative with a copy-number-high, low point-mutation profile.

hypotheses/2.description: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma in Fanconi anemia arises predominantly through an HPV-independent route in which endogenous aldehydes (acetaldehyde, formaldehyde) and replication stress in FA-deficient oral keratinocytes generate structural chromosomal variation and copy-number driven, low point-mutation-burden tumors, with premalignant leukoplakia as the visible intermediate. Competing hypotheses are an HPV-driven route and a chronic-inflammation or graft-versus-host-mediated route after transplantation.

evidence.snippet: At age 38, computerized tomography showed bilateral upper lobe fibrosis, lower lobe honeycombing, and bronchiectasis.
evidence.explanation: Seed reference; the single adult case on which the phenotype rests.

evidence.snippet: The pathogenic mechanism of lung involvement in FA may relate to oxidative injury and cytokine anomalies.
evidence.explanation: The mechanism is offered as conjecture by the case authors, not demonstrated; retained as the origin of the oxidative-cytokine hypothesis.

hypotheses/3.description: The rare interstitial lung disease of Fanconi anemia reflects oxidative injury and cytokine dysregulation in FA-deficient alveolar epithelium, analogous to the telomere-biology-disorder route to pulmonary fibrosis, rather than transplant conditioning, infection or an environmental exposure. A competing explanation is that the reported cases are post-transplant or treatment-related and not an intrinsic FA phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Absolute numbers of B cells and natural killer (NK) cells were reduced compared to controls
evidence.explanation: Seed reference; reduced NK and B cell numbers in children with FA.

evidence.snippet: this is the first report showing a defective degranulation mechanism leading to abnormal NK-cell cytotoxicity in FA-patients
evidence.explanation: Identifies a defined NK degranulation lesion behind the reduced cytotoxicity, supporting an intrinsic NK defect rather than a simple numeric deficit.

evidence.snippet: We performed a detailed immunologic assessment in a large FA cohort who have not undergone bone marrow transplantation or developed malignancies.
evidence.explanation: The cohort design excludes transplantation and malignancy, establishing that the NK and B cell abnormalities are not transplant consequences.

evidence.snippet: Fancc(-/-) B cells show a specific defect in IgG2a switch and impaired Ab-secreting cell (ASC) differentiation.
evidence.explanation: Cell-intrinsic B-lineage functional defect in a Fancc-null mouse with largely preserved steady-state hematopoiesis, the strongest evidence that the lymphoid defect is marrow-failure independent.

hypotheses/4.description: Fanconi anemia carries a quantitative and functional NK-cell and B-cell defect that is intrinsic to FA-deficient lymphoid progenitors or to their cytotoxic machinery, present before and independently of marrow failure and transplantation, rather than a simple consequence of pancytopenia. Candidate mechanisms are p53-mediated loss of lymphoid progenitors, defective perforin and granzyme loading, and impaired proliferative response to activation.

evidence.snippet: The association of moyamoya disease with FA is uncommon, and is rarely reported in the literature.
evidence.explanation: Seed reference; the association rests on a handful of case reports and has no proposed mechanism.

hypotheses/5.description: The moyamoya phenomenon reported in Fanconi anemia reflects an intrinsic arteriopathy of FA-deficient vascular smooth muscle or endothelium, possibly sharing the RNF213-independent progenitor-apoptosis route of other FA structural anomalies, rather than a coincidental association or a consequence of cranial irradiation or transplantation.

open_questions/0.rationale: The phenotype is explained in the pathograph only through the generic Endocrine Gland Dysfunction node, which was built around pituitary hypoplasia. The childhood OGTT study shows a secretory defect with normal HOMA-IR, which pituitary hypoplasia does not explain. No islet-level study of FA-deficient beta cells is cited in the entry.

open_questions/1.rationale: Every malformation in the entry routes through p53-Dependent Developmental Progenitor Arrest and Apoptosis and then Congenital Structural Anomalies. That chain states that progenitors arrest or die, not why the radial ray, kidney, ear and heart are the organs that fail. The effector node was widened from apoptosis-only to arrest-and-apoptosis on FA hematopoietic evidence; no FA limb-bud measurement exists. A limb or digit serial-homology module conformance would give the radial ray story a specific developmental step once the field-level mechanism is established.

open_questions/2.rationale: The most frequent solid tumor of FA is connected to the pathograph only through a generic epithelial susceptibility node. The entry models an HPV route and an aldehyde route to hematopoietic stem cell loss, but not an aldehyde route in oral epithelium, and does not state which route dominates.

open_questions/3.rationale: The phenotype rests on a single adult case report that proposed oxidative injury and cytokine dysregulation without mechanistic data, in a patient with a smoking history, recent prednisone and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole exposure. It has no incoming edge in the pathograph and none was added because no mechanism node is justified by the evidence in hand.

open_questions/4.rationale: The immune phenotypes are described as independent of transplantation and of marrow failure, so wiring them to Bone Marrow Failure would misstate the evidence. Recurrent Infections was connected as a sequela of Neutropenia only; the intrinsic lymphoid route is left unexplained pending a mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The association of moyamoya disease with FA is uncommon, and is rarely reported in the literature.
evidence.explanation: The authors themselves characterise the association as rare and unexplained.

open_questions/5.rationale: Two case reports with no proposed mechanism. No edge was added; the phenotype stays disconnected until a vascular mechanism is supported.

open_questions/6.rationale: These phenotypes have no mechanism node and were deliberately left disconnected: the cited cohort study frames them as an under-recognized part of the disease burden in the first generation of adult survivors, not as a biological consequence of FA pathway loss. No cited study separates the disease-burden effect from a candidate biological contribution, so fabricating a mechanism edge would overstate the evidence.

open_questions/7.rationale: Live queries of the HPO annotation API and the Monarch Initiative API on 2026-09-13, logged in the OpenScientist report for the intrinsic lymphoid defect hypothesis, returned no NK, B cell, immunoglobulin or immunodeficiency term for Fanconi anemia at disease level (OMIM:227650, MONDO:0009215) or for any FA gene; the only immune-adjacent term is decreased neutrophil count. Candidate terms are Reduced natural killer cell count (HP:0040218), which this entry already binds, and Immunodeficiency (HP:0002721). This is an upstream annotation gap, not a dismech edit; it needs a request on the HPO annotation tracker with the cohort citations recorded on the Reduced Natural Killer Cell Count phenotype.

open_questions/8.rationale: These manifestations are reported in registries (Orphanet occasional annotations) or case reports, but the literature does not identify a mediating mechanism connecting them to marrow failure, malformation, endocrine, or cancer arms of FA pathophysiology. They are recorded without causal edges rather than wired speculatively; several (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis, weight loss) may be secondary to treatment, transplant, or advanced disease.

open_questions/9.rationale: PMID:31558676 reports associations of splice-site variants with developmental delay and CNS anomalies, but does not establish that the anomalies cause the delay. The MRI study PMID:26369989 documents structural abnormalities rather than a causal cognitive association. The FA-S review PMID:38146508 reports intellectual disability, but notes neuroanatomical anomalies in only two siblings and raises a separate undiagnosed condition as an alternative. Neither phenotype is therefore assigned a structural-brain causal edge.

open_questions/10.rationale: Orphanet documents cranial nerve paralysis without identifying a causative developmental lesion. PMID:32822789 distinguishes skin-fold freckle-like macules from sun-exposed freckling and reports an association of the latter with voriconazole exposure (OR 15.25), a phototoxicity route rather than a developmental one. These observations do not establish embryonic melanocyte progenitor loss as the cause of freckling or congenital structural anomalies as the cause of cranial nerve paralysis. The Skin Pigmentation Changes -> Freckling edge is therefore not drawn; it is the one edge from that node whose target the cited series attributes substantially to drug exposure.

open_questions/11.rationale: PMID:17426088 and PMID:19622403 describe obesity and dyslipidemia in FA endocrine surveys. Their co-occurrence with endocrinopathy does not establish gland dysfunction as the cause; the prior edges stated that mediation was unknown while treating the association as causal, so no Endocrine Gland Dysfunction edge is drawn to either phenotype. The Obesity -> Abnormal Circulating Lipid Concentration sequela is retained and is a narrower claim: it asserts the ordinary adiposity-to-dyslipidemia route within the cohort's metabolic-syndrome cluster, not an FA-pathway mechanism, which is what this gap still asks for.

evidence.snippet: autosomal dominant D187N or D187Y mutations compromise Ca(2+) binding in domain 2 of gelsolin, allowing domain 2 to sample unfolded conformations
evidence.explanation: Establishes the precise molecular defect - loss of calcium binding in domain 2 - and its immediate structural consequence.

evidence.snippet: It is the first and so-far only known disorder caused by a gelsolin gene defect, namely a G654A or G654T mutation.
evidence.explanation: Gives the causal variants at nucleotide level and the uniqueness of the gene-disease pair.

steps/1.description: The initiating lesion. D187N or D187Y substitutions compromise calcium binding in gelsolin domain 2. The variant does not directly destabilise the whole protein into an aggregation-prone state; it removes the calcium coordination that holds domain 2 folded, so the domain begins to sample unfolded conformations.

evidence.snippet: When domain 2 is unfolded, gelsolin is subject to aberrant furin endoproteolysis as it passes through the Golgi on its way to the extracellular space.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the intracellular protease, the compartment, and the conditional nature of the cleavage.

steps/2.description: An unfolded domain 2 exposes a site that furin cleaves while the protein is passing through the Golgi on its way to secretion. This is the step that converts a folding defect into a proteolysis problem, and it is compartment-specific: the wild-type protein traverses the same pathway untouched.

evidence.snippet: The resulting C-terminal 68 kDa fragment (C68) is susceptible to extracellular endoproteolytic events, possibly mediated by a matrix metalloprotease, affording 8 and 5 kDa amyloidogenic fragments of gelsolin.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the second, extracellular cleavage and identifies the fragments that form the amyloid. Note the authors hedge the responsible protease ("possibly"), which is preserved in the description.

steps/3.description: The furin cut yields a C-terminal 68 kDa fragment (C68), which is then cut again outside the cell - probably by a matrix metalloprotease - to give the 8 and 5 kDa fragments that are the actual amyloid precursor. Two proteases, two compartments, and only the final products are amyloidogenic. This node is what the entry substitutes for the amyloidogenesis module's generic precursor node.

evidence.snippet: These amyloidogenic fragments deposit systemically, causing a variety of symptoms including corneal lattice dystrophy and neurodegeneration.
evidence.explanation: Links the fragments to systemic deposition and to the two cardinal manifestations.

evidence.snippet: The gelsolin gene defect causes expression of variant gelsolin, followed by systemic deposition of gelsolin amyloid (AGel) in HGA patients
evidence.explanation: Independent statement of systemic AGel deposition as the pathological process.

steps/4.description: The fragments deposit as AGel amyloid systemically, with a striking tissue preference for cornea, cranial and peripheral nerves, and skin. Why those tissues rather than the heart, which dominates ATTR and AL, is not explained by the mechanism above.

evidence.snippet: The diagnostic triad includes corneal lattice dystrophy (type 2), progressive bilateral facial paralysis, and cutis laxa.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the three cardinal features that define the clinical syndrome.

steps/5.description: The clinical endpoint, dominated by the diagnostic triad. Cranial nerve involvement is progressive and measurable: in a series of 29 patients undergoing facial corrective surgery, facial paralysis was studied electroneurophysiologically, and the disease is characterised by progressive bilateral facial paralysis rather than a static deficit.

evidence.snippet: FAF appears to be caused by a gain-of-toxic function associated with gelsolin fragment amyloidogenesis
evidence.explanation: States the gain-of-toxic-function conclusion directly, which is why this entry does not curate a competing loss-of-function model.

evidence.snippet: gelsolin knockout mice exhibit a normal development and lifespan, exhibiting only a mild prolonged bleeding time phenotype and abnormally slowly migrating neutrophils and fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: The knockout evidence against a loss-of-function contribution: removing gelsolin entirely does not reproduce the disease.

evidence.snippet: It is the first and so-far only known disorder caused by a gelsolin gene defect, namely a G654A or G654T mutation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the causal gene-disease relationship and the specific variants.

evidence.snippet: One copy of the mutant allele appears to result in complete penetrance of FAF.
evidence.explanation: Establishes complete penetrance in heterozygotes, which is why the entry does not hedge the genotype-phenotype relationship.

evidence.snippet: Gelsolin is a principal actin-modulating protein, implicated in multiple biological processes, also in the nervous system, e.g. axonal transport, myelination, neurite outgrowth, and neuroprotection.
evidence.explanation: Curated as INDIRECT because it establishes gelsolin's normal neural functions without demonstrating that their loss contributes to this disease - the open question noted in the association text.

evidence.snippet: In HGA, specific therapy is not yet available but correct diagnosis enables adequate symptomatic treatment which decisively improves the quality of life in these patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the absence of specific therapy and the value of symptomatic care.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Management is symptomatic - ophthalmic care for the corneal disease, and facial corrective surgery for the paralysis, which a published series of 29 patients underwent. The cited review is explicit that correct diagnosis matters even absent specific therapy, because adequate symptomatic treatment substantially improves quality of life. No target_mechanisms link is asserted: nothing available acts on any node of the mechanism above.

treatments/1.description: Autosomal dominant counselling with a 50% transmission risk. Relevant across a wide and widening geographic range, not only in the Finnish founder population.

evidence.snippet: amyloidogenesis is observed only in tissues synthesizing human D187N gelsolin, despite the presence of the 68 kDa cleavage product circulating in the blood, suggesting that local synthesis is required for amyloid fragment formation and/or deposition
evidence.explanation: The local-synthesis hypothesis, and the reason this gap is a question about generalisation to humans rather than an absence of any candidate mechanism.

open_questions/0.rationale: The disease is defined by a cornea-nerve-skin triad, while the heart, the dominant target in both ATTR and AL, is not a cardinal feature - and the precursor is a plasma protein whose fragments enter the circulation, so systemic availability alone predicts the wrong distribution. There is one leading hypothesis rather than a blank: the D187N transgenic mouse deposits amyloid only in tissues that themselves synthesise the mutant gelsolin, despite circulating C68 being present throughout, which argues that local synthesis rather than circulating precursor governs where deposition happens. What is open is whether that generalises to human tissue distribution, since muscle is the major source of plasma gelsolin while cornea and cranial nerve are not obviously so. Competing explanations remain live: local availability of the second, extracellular protease (MT1-MMP and possibly others), tissue-specific extracellular matrix components that nucleate these particular fragments, or slow clearance in poorly vascularised tissue such as cornea. Which is right matters therapeutically, because a treatment aimed at the circulating fragment and one aimed at local synthesis or deposition are different drugs.

evidence.snippet: the discovery that the pathological changes in atypical FTLD with ubiquitinated inclusions, neuronal intermediate filament inclusion disease, and basophilic inclusion body disease are immunoreactive for the fused in sarcoma (FUS) protein, resulting in the creation of a new molecular subgroup (FTLD-FUS)
evidence.explanation: Establishes FTLD-FUS as a distinct, tau/TDP-43-negative molecular subgroup of frontotemporal lobar degeneration.

steps/1.description: A minority of FTD cases are tau- and TDP-43-negative. Within that heterogeneous group (which also includes CHMP2B-associated FTLD-UPS), the cases whose inclusions are immunoreactive for FUS (fused in sarcoma) constitute FTLD-FUS, completing the TDP-43 / tau / FUS molecular triad underlying FTD.

evidence.snippet: TDP-43 is typically a nuclear protein, and its aggregation and cytoplasmic translocation are thought to represent major steps in the pathogenesis of FTLD due to TDP-43 proteinopathy (FTLD-TDP).
evidence.explanation: This confirms that TDP-43 aggregation and mislocalization are central to the pathogenesis of FTLD-TDP, a major subtype of frontotemporal dementia.

steps/2.description: TAR DNA-binding protein of 43 kDa (TDP-43) is the main ubiquitinated protein in tau-negative frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD-TDP), accounting for over 50% of FTD cases. TDP-43 is typically a nuclear protein, and its aggregation and cytoplasmic translocation are thought to represent major pathogenic steps. The abnormal accumulation leads to neuronal dysfunction and death.

evidence.snippet: PiD is the least common FTLD-tau characterized by neuronal Pick bodies in a stereotypic neuroanatomical distribution.
evidence.explanation: This confirms Pick's disease (PiD), with its characteristic Pick bodies, as one of the FTLD-tau subtypes underlying the tau proteinopathy arm of FTD.

steps/3.description: FTLD-tau is characterized by accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, accounting for approximately 45% of FTD cases. This includes Pick's disease with characteristic Pick bodies. The tau pathology disrupts microtubule function and causes neuronal degeneration primarily in frontal and temporal regions.

evidence.snippet: MAPT patients were younger than other groups, and showed more frequent behavioural disinhibition, repetitive and stereotyped behaviours, semantic impairment and temporal predominance of atrophy.
evidence.explanation: This demonstrates the genotype-specific patterns of brain atrophy and their relationship to clinical phenotypes in frontotemporal dementia.

evidence.snippet: All VRS yielded higher atrophy in bvFTD than in PPD patients. The Orbitofrontal, the Anterior-Temporal, and the Fronto-Insula scales were the strongest discriminators.
evidence.explanation: Multicenter study identifying specific atrophy patterns (orbitofrontal, anterior-temporal, fronto-insular regions) as diagnostic biomarkers for distinguishing bvFTD from primary psychiatric disorder using visual rating scales.

steps/4.description: Progressive neuronal loss and atrophy predominantly affecting the frontal and temporal lobes, with patterns varying by genetic subtype. MAPT mutations show temporal predominance, while GRN and C9orf72 mutations may show more variable patterns. This structural degeneration underlies the behavioral and language deficits.

evidence.snippet: We observed that biological changes and intracortical facilitation transmission abnormalities significantly antecede the emergence of clinical symptoms of at least 3 decades.
evidence.explanation: Supports long presymptomatic neurobiological change in genetic FTD, but does not directly quantify neuronal death in the quoted text.

steps/5.description: Progressive loss of neurons in frontal and temporal cortices due to protein aggregation toxicity, leading to brain atrophy and functional decline. The neurodegeneration progresses over years to decades, with biomarker changes detectable up to 30 years before symptom onset in genetic cases.

evidence.snippet: MAPT patients were younger than other groups, and showed more frequent behavioural disinhibition, repetitive and stereotyped behaviours, semantic impairment and temporal predominance of atrophy.
evidence.explanation: This confirms that behavioral disinhibition and repetitive stereotyped behaviors are core clinical features of genetic FTD, particularly in MAPT mutations.

evidence.snippet: GRN patients were older at death and more likely to present with non-fluent aphasia.
evidence.explanation: This demonstrates that non-fluent aphasia is a characteristic presenting feature in patients with GRN mutations causing frontotemporal dementia.

evidence.snippet: MAPT patients were younger than other groups, and showed more frequent behavioural disinhibition, repetitive and stereotyped behaviours, semantic impairment and temporal predominance of atrophy.
evidence.explanation: This confirms the distinct clinical and anatomical phenotype associated with MAPT mutations in frontotemporal dementia.

evidence.snippet: carriers exhibited pronounced impairments in semantic knowledge and social cognition
evidence.explanation: Digital cognitive assessment of 569 Genetic FTD Initiative participants shows MAPT carriers have a semantic-knowledge and social-cognition predominant cognitive profile.

genes/0.notes: Microtubule-associated protein tau gene on chromosome 17q21. Mutations lead to FTLD-tau pathology. Patients show earlier onset, prominent behavioral disinhibition, stereotyped behaviors, and temporal lobe predominance of atrophy. On digital cognitive assessment, MAPT carriers show a semantic-knowledge and social-cognition predominant profile.

evidence.snippet: GRN patients were older at death and more likely to present with non-fluent aphasia.
evidence.explanation: This demonstrates the characteristic clinical presentation of GRN-related FTD with language deficits.

evidence.snippet: Presymptomatic carriers of GRN and C9orf72 mutations, the most frequent genetic causes of frontotemporal lobar degeneration, represent the optimal target population for the development of disease-modifying drugs.
evidence.explanation: This confirms GRN as one of the two most common genetic causes of FTD.

evidence.snippet: carriers demonstrated marked deficits in executive function and processing speed, particularly at symptomatic stages
evidence.explanation: Digital cognitive assessment of 569 Genetic FTD Initiative participants shows GRN carriers have an executive-function and processing-speed predominant cognitive profile.

genes/1.notes: Progranulin gene on chromosome 17q21. Haploinsufficiency leads to FTLD-TDP pathology. Patients more likely to present with non-fluent aphasia and are older at symptom onset. GRN and C9orf72 are the most frequent genetic causes. On digital cognitive assessment, GRN carriers show an executive-function and processing-speed predominant profile, most marked at symptomatic stages.

evidence.snippet: C9orf72 patients alone showed a co-occurrence of ALS. They showed more psychotic symptoms and irrational behaviour, yet were more often reported clinically as socially appropriate and warm.
evidence.explanation: This highlights the distinctive clinical features of C9orf72-related FTD including the frequent association with ALS and unique behavioral profile.

evidence.snippet: Presymptomatic carriers of GRN and C9orf72 mutations, the most frequent genetic causes of frontotemporal lobar degeneration, represent the optimal target population for the development of disease-modifying drugs.
evidence.explanation: This confirms C9orf72 as one of the most common genetic causes of FTD.

evidence.snippet: mutation carriers showed the earliest and broadest deficits across all cognitive domains
evidence.explanation: Digital cognitive assessment of 569 Genetic FTD Initiative participants shows C9orf72 carriers have the earliest and broadest cognitive impairment of the three genetic groups.

genes/2.notes: Hexanucleotide (GGGGCC) repeat expansion on chromosome 9p21. Most common genetic cause of FTD. Causes FTLD-TDP pathology. Unique features include co-occurrence with ALS, psychotic symptoms, and paradoxically preserved social warmth. On digital cognitive assessment, C9orf72 carriers show the earliest and broadest deficits of the three genetic groups, spanning all six cognitive domains.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying treatments currently available. Management focuses on behavioral symptoms with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for compulsive behaviors and agitation, and non-pharmacological approaches including behavioral interventions and caregiver support.

treatments/1.description: Speech therapy interventions for patients with language-variant FTD to maintain communication abilities and quality of life for as long as possible.

evidence.snippet: The Y99C mutation does not decrease the ability of GCAP-1 to activate RetGC. However, RetGC stimulated by the Y99C GCAP-1 remains active even at Ca2+ concentration above 1 microM. Hence, the cyclase becomes constitutively active within the whole physiologically relevant range of free Ca2+ concentrations.
evidence.explanation: Dizhoor et al. biochemically demonstrate that the Y99C GCAP1 mutant fails to lose its RetGC-activating conformation at high (dark-adapted) Ca2+, the direct molecular basis of loss of calcium-dependent inhibitory control.

evidence.snippet: The mutant was less sensitive to changes in free Ca2+, resulting in a constitutively active form under physiological Ca2+-concentration, showed significantly higher activation rates than the wildtype (90-fold versus 20-fold) and interacted with an higher apparent affinity with its target guanylate cyclase.
evidence.explanation: Vocke et al. show the L176F GCAP1 variant is biochemically less Ca2+-sensitive and binds RetGC with higher affinity, reproducing the same loss-of-calcium-control mechanism in a second, independently identified variant.

evidence.snippet: These result in persistent stimulation of RetGC, excess cGMP levels in the dark and photoreceptor apoptosis secondary to Ca2+ dysregulation.
evidence.explanation: Gill et al. summarize the shared consequence of the GUCA1A gain-of-function alleles, tying the EF-hand lesion to persistent RetGC stimulation. Classified OTHER because this is a narrative review synthesizing published cohorts rather than reporting primary observations.

steps/1.description: Dominant missense variants in GUCA1A cluster in the EF-hand calcium-binding loops of GCAP1 (e.g. EF3 for the founding p.Tyr99Cys variant, EF4 for p.Asp144Gly), impairing the protein's ability to sense rising dark-adapted Ca2+ and switch into its RetGC-inhibiting conformation. The founding p.Tyr99Cys variant does not decrease GCAP1's ability to activate RetGC, but the resulting RetGC-GCAP1 complex remains active even at Ca2+ concentrations above 1 microM, well into the physiological dark-adapted range, rather than being suppressed as normal GCAP1 would suppress it. Other variants (p.Asn104His, p.Leu176Phe, p.Asp144Gly) act through related biophysical mechanisms: impaired Ca2+ sensitivity, altered Mg2+/Ca2+ exchange kinetics, or increased binding affinity for RetGC, all converging on loss of the normal Ca2+-dependent brake on cyclase activation.

evidence.snippet: The altered interaction with GC would cause hyper-activity of the enzyme at both low and high Ca2+ levels, which would ultimately lead to toxic accumulation of cGMP and Ca2+ in the photoreceptor outer segment, thus triggering cell death.
evidence.explanation: Biasi et al. directly link the N104H GCAP1 variant's hyperactivation of guanylate cyclase to downstream toxic cGMP/Ca2+ accumulation, connecting the enzymatic hyperactivity node to the downstream calcium overload node.

evidence.snippet: Y99C GCAP1 shifted the Ca2+ sensitivity of the guanylyl cyclase in photoreceptors, keeping it partially active at 250 nM free Ca2+, the normal resting Ca2+ concentration in darkness.
evidence.explanation: Olshevskaya et al. show in vivo that the Y99C transgene leaves the cyclase active at the resting dark Ca2+ concentration, confirming in a whole retina the set-point failure demonstrated biochemically.

steps/2.description: Constitutively activating mutant GCAP1 continues to stimulate retinal guanylate cyclase (RetGC1 and, for some variants, also RetGC2) even at Ca2+ concentrations characteristic of the dark-adapted state, when wild-type GCAP1 would normally suppress the enzyme. This produces chronically elevated cGMP synthesis that is no longer coupled to the light-dependent Ca2+ signal, independent of the ambient light state.

evidence.snippet: The enhanced activity of the cyclase in the dark increased cyclic nucleotide-gated channel activity and elevated the rod outer segment Ca2+ concentration in darkness
evidence.explanation: Olshevskaya et al. measured the outer-segment Ca2+ rise directly in the Y99C transgenic retina, establishing that the channel opening and the calcium overload are real consequences of the cyclase lesion and not only an inference from biochemistry.

evidence.snippet: The altered interaction with GC would cause hyper-activity of the enzyme at both low and high Ca2+ levels, which would ultimately lead to toxic accumulation of cGMP and Ca2+ in the photoreceptor outer segment, thus triggering cell death.
evidence.explanation: Biasi et al. name toxic cGMP and Ca2+ accumulation in the outer segment as the step between cyclase hyperactivity and photoreceptor death.

steps/3.description: Chronically elevated cGMP holds cyclic nucleotide-gated channels open independent of the light state, so Ca2+ and Na+ enter the outer segment continuously and free Ca2+ rises above its normal dark level. This is the branch point at which a phototransduction set-point lesion becomes a degenerative rather than a stationary disease.

evidence.snippet: Ten of 13 subjects had subnormal LA 30-Hz or LA 3 (single-flash) ERGs
evidence.explanation: Allon et al. quantify reduced cone-driven light-adapted ERG responses in the majority of tested patients, the functional readout of failed cone light-response generation.

evidence.snippet: there was an additional LA 30-Hz ERG delay in the 5 with the smallest LA responses
evidence.explanation: The flicker peak-time delay in the most severely affected patients is the timing abnormality that distinguishes a recovery defect from a simple loss of responding cones.

steps/4.description: Loss of the Ca2+-gated cyclase brake degrades the cone light response itself, separately from the degenerative arm. Cone-driven full-field ERG amplitudes are reduced in most affected patients, and in the most severely affected the 30-Hz flicker response is also delayed, which is the timing signature of a recovery defect rather than a pure amplitude loss.

evidence.snippet: the abnormal electroretinogram recorded in this patient also suggested that the dysregulation of the GCAP1-cyclase complex further propagates to the synaptic terminal, thereby altering the ON-pathway related to the b-wave generation
evidence.explanation: Marino et al. report ERG evidence in a patient carrying a double GCAP1 substitution (N104K/G105R) that dysregulated GCAP1-RetGC signaling also disturbs synaptic transmission to ON-bipolar cells.

evidence.snippet: Severe alterations of the electroretinogram were observed under both scotopic and photopic conditions, with a negative pattern and abnormally attenuated b-wave component.
evidence.explanation: The negative ERG waveform with attenuated b-wave is the specific electrophysiological signature of inner-retinal transmission failure rather than outer-segment loss alone.

steps/5.description: In some patients the dysregulated GCAP1-cyclase complex disturbs signaling at the photoreceptor synaptic terminal rather than only in the outer segment, producing an attenuated b-wave and an electronegative ERG waveform that indicate an ON-pathway transmission defect.

evidence.snippet: However, the photoreceptors in these mice degenerated, and the rate of the cell loss increased with the level of the transgene expression, unlike in transgenic mice that overexpressed normal GCAP1.
evidence.explanation: Dose-dependent photoreceptor loss with the mutant but not the wild-type transgene establishes that degeneration follows from the variant rather than from GCAP1 overexpression as such.

evidence.snippet: The relative preservation of rod responses in most GUCA1A-associated progressive retinal dystrophies is attributed to greater GCAP1 expression in cones.
evidence.explanation: Gill et al. give the reason cones are affected first, which is the claim this node makes about the cell-type selectivity of the degeneration. Classified OTHER because this is a narrative review.

steps/6.description: Persistent calcium and cGMP elevation triggers photoreceptor cell death. Cones bear the earliest and most severe toxicity because GCAP1 expression is higher in cones and cone recovery kinetics depend on it more heavily, with later, more variable rod and macular RPE involvement depending on the specific variant.

evidence.snippet: In the latter patient, the nature and progression of symptoms were still more in keeping with a cone-rod, rather than a rod-cone, dystrophy, and other family members did not show the pigmentary changes.
evidence.explanation: Even in the patient with peripheral pigmentary change, the course stayed cone-rod. This is the evidence for scoping this node as variable involvement rather than as a rod-degeneration arm.

evidence.snippet: The relative preservation of rod responses in most GUCA1A-associated progressive retinal dystrophies is attributed to greater GCAP1 expression in cones.
evidence.explanation: Gives the reason rods are relatively spared, which is the same claim this node makes from the other side: rods carry the lesion but at lower GCAP1 dose. Classified OTHER because this is a narrative review.

steps/7.description: GCAP1 is expressed in rods as well as cones, so the rod population is not immune to the same cGMP and calcium set-point lesion. Rod involvement is the exception rather than the rule: dark-adapted rod-specific ERGs were normal in almost every tested patient, and peripheral pigmentary change appeared in 2 of 19. Where it occurs it marks the cone-rod end of the phenotypic range, not a conversion to a rod-first disease.

evidence.snippet: Most had progressive visual loss and electrophysiologic evidence of cone dystrophy.
evidence.explanation: Allon et al. report progressive visual loss as the predominant clinical course in the largest reported GUCA1A cohort (19 patients, 14 families).

evidence.snippet: The mean (SD) age of onset of symptoms was 23 (17) years (range, 5–74 years).
evidence.explanation: Source for the onset descriptor: mean age of symptom onset and its full reported range in the same cohort.

steps/8.description: Progressive decline in central visual acuity is the dominant presenting and progressive feature of GUCA1A-related retinopathy, correlating with patient age across longitudinal follow-up. Central vision deficits were reported by 17 of 19 patients (89.5%) in the largest cohort.

evidence.snippet: Acuities ranged from 0.00 logMAR to no light perception.
evidence.explanation: Allon et al. document the full range of visual acuity severity observed across the GUCA1A cohort, from near-normal to no light perception.

steps/9.description: Visual acuity at presentation is variable but declines with age and can range from near-normal to no light perception in advanced disease; logMAR acuity correlates with patient age across longitudinal follow-up.

evidence.snippet: Overall, across the entire duration of follow-up, 17 patients (89.5%) reported central vision deficits, 16 patients (84.2%) described color vision deficits, 15 (78.9%) reported some degree of photophobia
evidence.explanation: 84.2% of the cohort described color vision deficits, which places the frequency in the VERY_FREQUENT band (80-99%).

evidence.snippet: Thirteen patients (68.4%) described poor color discrimination as their initial symptom
evidence.explanation: Color vision impairment is also the commonest presenting symptom, which is why it is treated as the early feature of the disease.

steps/10.description: Dyschromatopsia is the characteristic early feature of GUCA1A-related retinopathy, reflecting the cone-predominant nature of the underlying photoreceptor dysfunction. It affected 16 of 19 patients (84.2%) over follow-up and was the presenting complaint in 13 (68.4%).

evidence.snippet: Overall, across the entire duration of follow-up, 17 patients (89.5%) reported central vision deficits, 16 patients (84.2%) described color vision deficits, 15 (78.9%) reported some degree of photophobia
evidence.explanation: 78.9% of the GUCA1A cohort reported photophobia, which sets the FREQUENT band (30-79%) just below the VERY_FREQUENT threshold.

evidence.snippet: These disorders typically present with progressive loss of central vision, colour vision disturbance and photophobia.
evidence.explanation: Supporting class-level characterization of photophobia as a typical presenting feature of progressive cone and cone-rod dystrophies, of which GUCA1A is one of the four commonest causes. Classified OTHER because this is a narrative review, and it is a second item behind the GUCA1A-specific figure rather than the source of the frequency band.

steps/11.description: Light sensitivity is a typical symptom of GUCA1A-related cone and cone-rod dystrophy, reported by 15 of 19 patients (78.9%) in the largest cohort.

evidence.snippet: Electrophysiology (n = 13) was consistent with cone dystrophy (n = 11) or macular dystrophy (n = 2).
evidence.explanation: Allon et al. report electrophysiological findings consistent with cone dystrophy in the large majority of tested patients in the GUCA1A cohort.

evidence.snippet: ERG studies characteristically show reduced cone single-flash and flicker amplitudes with a normal implicit time
evidence.explanation: Describes the characteristic GUCA1A ERG signature. Classified OTHER because this is a narrative review. Note that the Allon cohort did find a flicker peak-time delay in its five most severely affected patients, so the normal implicit time described here holds for milder disease and is not universal.

steps/12.description: Electrophysiology in GUCA1A-related retinopathy is consistent with cone dystrophy in most patients, with a subset showing a macular dystrophy pattern; occasional patients show additional abnormalities in the ON-pathway b-wave component suggesting a synaptic transmission component.

evidence.snippet: Maculopathy was evident in all individuals on OCT imaging.
evidence.explanation: Structural macular involvement was universal (19/19) on OCT, which sets the VERY_FREQUENT band. The macular-dystrophy ERG pattern seen in 2 of 13 tested patients is a separate, rarer electrophysiological finding and is recorded on the electroretinogram phenotype, not here.

evidence.snippet: Optical coherence tomography showed irregularity and then loss of the central ellipsoid zone.
evidence.explanation: Documents the progressive structural sequence on OCT underlying the atrophy.

steps/13.description: Maculopathy was present on OCT in every patient in the largest cohort. Imaging shows progressive irregularity of the central ellipsoid zone, then partial disruption, then complete loss of the layer, which is the structural correlate of central cone photoreceptor degeneration.

evidence.snippet: Visual field tests, where performed (four patients), demonstrated central and paracentral scotomas.

open_questions/0.rationale: The multilineage stem cell dysfunction node is supported by MODEL_ORGANISM evidence in which DNMT3A gain-of-function "recapitulate[s] age-related gains in DNA methylation ... and phenocopy[ies] aspects of aging in humans and mice." That model frames the readout as an aging phenotype (reduced stem cell output, lineage skewing, hematological/bone/metabolic decline). HESJAS, however, is a pediatric developmental disorder, and the published human case material documents microcephaly, growth failure, and developmental delay rather than accelerated-aging multilineage failure. It is therefore mechanistically uncertain whether the stem-cell-dysfunction arm operates as a clinically relevant pathway in human HESJAS at the ages so far described, or whether it is a model-system correlate whose human-disease relevance is age- or lineage-dependent. This is a translational-validity gap, not an absence of evidence, so it is recorded as HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH rather than KNOWLEDGE_GAP.

steps/0.description: Trypanosoma brucei expresses a single Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG) at a time from a large genomic repertoire, forming a dense protective surface coat. Periodic switching to an antigenically distinct VSG allows each new parasite subpopulation to escape the antibody response raised against the previous coat, so a relapsing wave of parasites survives each round of antibody-mediated clearance. steps/1.description: The initiating lesion is biallelic loss of function of IRF8. steps/2.description: Without IRF8, the mononuclear phagocyte lineage fails to develop. Circulating monocytes are absent and both conventional and plasmacytoid dendritic cells are absent from blood, while other lymphoid subsets are largely preserved. This is a developmental block in myelopoiesis rather than a signalling defect, and it defines the cellular lesion of IMD32B.

steps/3.description: The block in mononuclear phagocyte development is accompanied by an expansion of the granulocytic compartment. IRF8 normally restrains granulopoiesis, and its loss diverts myeloid output toward neutrophils, producing a striking granulocytic hyperplasia and peripheral neutrophilia alongside the monocyte and dendritic cell aplasia. The expanded granulocytes are not merely increased in number: in the biallelic syndrome they are also consistently dysplastic and hypofunctional.

evidence.snippet: Cell-specific gene expression was widely disturbed in interferon- and IRF8-regulated transcripts.

steps/4.description: Biallelic (complete) IRF8 deficiency is not confined to the mononuclear phagocyte compartment: it produces widespread immune dysregulation across other hematopoietic lineages. Natural killer cell development and maturation are arrested; TH1, TH17 and CD8+ memory T-cell differentiation is reduced with loss of CXCR3; and B-cell development is impaired with fewer memory cells, reduced class-switching and reduced somatic hypermutation. The T-cell component is at least partly secondary to the absent antigen-presenting compartment, whereas the NK and B-cell defects reflect the broader roles of IRF8. This axis distinguishes the complete recessive syndrome from the milder dominant IRF8 disorder.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss-of-function variants abolish RIPK1 protein. RIPK1 is a 75.9 kDa protein with an N-terminal kinase domain, a C-terminal death domain and an intermediate domain carrying a RIP homotypic interaction motif, and it is recruited with TRADD to TNFR1 to form signalling complex I. Because the protein carries both a scaffolding role and a kinase role, its complete absence removes two opposing functions simultaneously, which is why the resulting disease is not simply a loss of inflammation or a gain of it.

steps/2.description: Complex I normally routes the TNFR1 signal into NF-kappaB and MAPK activation, producing pro-inflammatory cytokines and promoting survival. In RIPK1-deficient cells both arms are blunted: MAPK activation and cytokine secretion are impaired. This is the immunodeficiency half of the disease.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replacing the haematopoietic compartment supplies lymphoid progenitors with intact RIPK1.

evidence.snippet: | family 3 | P4 | Arab | F | 460-133_689-244del | DELexon5 | 2 yrs. | LLLL | Y | N | N | Y | N | N | N | N | severe RSV bronchiolitis, recurrent OM | IVIG | Alive |
evidence.explanation: Table 1, patient P4: the `Treatments` column reads IVIG. The table legend expands the abbreviation.

evidence.snippet: Ab, antibiotics; AF, antifungal; AZA, azathioprine; CS, corticosteroids; IBD, inflammatory bowel disease; IFX, infliximab; IVIG, intravenous immunoglobulin
evidence.explanation: The legend that makes the treatment abbreviations in Table 1 readable, and the reason the rows quoted across this section can be interpreted at all.

treatments/1.description: Intravenous immunoglobulin is recorded for two of the fourteen recessive patients in the review's Table 1 (P4 and P14). It replaces the antibody output the B cell differentiation defect removes and is supportive rather than disease-directed: it does nothing about the autoinflammatory arm, and P14 died while receiving it.

evidence.snippet: | family 9 | P12 | North Africa | F | 1802G>A | C601Y | 3 mos. | LLLL | Y | N | N | N | N | N | N | Y | OM, tetany, perianal disease | Ab, AF, CS | Alive |
evidence.explanation: Table 1, patient P12: the `Treatments` column reads Ab, AF, CS, where CS is corticosteroids in the table legend.

treatments/2.description: Corticosteroids are recorded for four of the fourteen recessive patients (P5, P7, P9 and P12) in the review's Table 1, used against the inflammatory manifestations. No outcome is attributed to them in the table, and two of the four patients who received them died, so this records practice rather than efficacy.

treatments/3.description: Two of the fourteen recessive patients (P5 and P9) received azathioprine together with infliximab, antibiotics and corticosteroids, which is conventional inflammatory bowel disease management rather than anything specific to RIPK1. P5 died; P9 was alive at the time of writing. Azathioprine and infliximab are curated as separate treatments because their modalities differ and the slot takes one value, not because the source separates them.
