evidence.snippet: Personal history of febrile seizures and parasomnias were equally frequent (20%).
evidence.explanation: Establishes febrile seizures as a personal antecedent in a fifth of a rolandic epilepsy cohort. Two cautions apply. The support is indirect: a cohort prevalence shows the co-occurrence the edge posits, but does not itself demonstrate that a shared inherited susceptibility produces both, which is why the edge is typed INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES. And the authors describe this Colombian cohort as "clearly different from other cohorts", with earlier onset and unusually prevalent febrile seizures and parasomnias, so the 20% figure should not be read as a general SeLECTS prevalence.

edges/3.description: In a minority of children the same inherited seizure susceptibility is expressed earlier as febrile seizures, before the centrotemporal-spike epilepsy declares itself; febrile seizures are an antecedent of the syndrome rather than a consequence of its discharges.

evidence.snippet: epileptiform spikes can be triggered and promoted by either a reduced NMDA current or h-type current
evidence.explanation: A thalamocortical neural-mass model of rolandic epilepsy shows how altered excitability in the Rolandic circuit generates the NREM-sleep-activated spikes, the step this edge asserts. Evidence source is COMPUTATIONAL because the result comes from in silico simulation.

evidence.snippet: changes in inhibitory transmission in the thalamic reticular nucleus mediates an antagonistic dynamic between epileptiform spikes and spindles
evidence.explanation: Offers a mechanism for the sleep dependence specifically: the spikes compete for the same thalamocortical circuit that generates NREM sleep spindles.

edges/4.description: The hyperexcitable perirolandic cortex generates centrotemporal spikes, strongly activated by sleep.

evidence.snippet: Since seizures associated with rolandic spikes are infrequent and usually occur during sleep
evidence.explanation: Ictal video-EEG documents the seizures as the clinical counterpart of the rolandic spikes and shares their sleep predominance, which is what this edge asserts.

edges/5.description: The discharges manifest clinically as focal perirolandic seizures.

evidence.snippet: children with ECTS demonstrated significantly lower scores on neuropsychological tests across all cognitive factors compared to healthy controls
evidence.explanation: A meta-analysis of 42 case-control samples establishes that the cognitive dysfunction is real and measurable, so the target of this edge is well supported. Graded PARTIAL rather than SUPPORT because the same paper argues the deficits are pervasive rather than circumscribed, which cuts against calling them merely transient; the paper does not test whether the discharges cause them.

edges/6.description: Frequent epileptiform activity, especially in sleep, transiently disrupts language and cognitive networks.

evidence.snippet: The EEG shows characteristic high-voltage sharp waves in the centrotemporal regions, which are activated with drowsiness and sleep.
evidence.explanation: States both the scalp morphology and the sleep activation that this edge claims the discharges produce.

edges/7.description: The high-amplitude, sleep-activated centrotemporal spike-waves recorded on EEG are the direct scalp expression of these discharges.

evidence.snippet: The typical presentation is a partial seizure with parasthesias and tonic or clonic activity of the lower face
evidence.explanation: The syndrome's typical seizure is described as partial (focal) in onset, which is what this edge asserts.

edges/8.description: The perirolandic seizure is a focal-onset seizure, characteristically nocturnal and arising in mid-childhood.

evidence.snippet: characterized by paresthesia in his left face, blocking of speech, and drooling
evidence.explanation: Ictal video-EEG documentation of unilateral facial paresthesia opening a recorded rolandic seizure.

evidence.snippet: The typical presentation is a partial seizure with parasthesias and tonic or clonic activity of the lower face
evidence.explanation: Places the paresthesia in the lower face, matching the perirolandic onset zone.

edges/9.description: Onset in the perirolandic somatosensory cortex produces the unilateral perioral or intraoral paresthesia that commonly opens the seizure.

evidence.snippet: characterized by eye and perioral deviation, and speech arrest at age of 7
evidence.explanation: Ictal video-EEG documentation of speech arrest during a recorded rolandic seizure.

evidence.snippet: associated with drooling and dysarthria
evidence.explanation: Names dysarthria as part of the syndrome's typical seizure.

edges/10.description: Involvement of the oropharyngeal motor strip produces speech arrest and anarthria/dysarthria during the seizure.

evidence.snippet: associated with drooling and dysarthria
evidence.explanation: Names drooling as part of the syndrome's typical seizure.

evidence.snippet: characterized by paresthesia in his left face, blocking of speech, and drooling
evidence.explanation: Ictal video-EEG documentation of drooling during a recorded rolandic seizure.

edges/11.description: The same oropharyngeal perirolandic involvement produces the near-defining ictal hypersalivation and drooling.

evidence.snippet: Seizures commonly occur at night and may become secondarily generalized.
evidence.explanation: Secondary generalization is the pre-2017 term for the focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic evolution this edge asserts.

edges/12.description: A focal perirolandic seizure may propagate bilaterally and evolve into a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.

evidence.snippet: We found linguistic deficits during the course of epilepsy but also persistent deficits in children in remission, suggesting possible long-term effects.
evidence.explanation: Supports the link between the active epilepsy and language impairment, and reports deficits persisting in children already in remission, which is why this edge does not claim the deficits fully resolve.

evidence.snippet: Reading performance is impaired in children with rolandic epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: Quantified literacy impairment, the learning-difficulty half of this phenotype.

edges/13.description: The dysfunction presents clinically as specific language and learning difficulties during the active epilepsy period. Whether it fully resolves with seizure remission is not settled - deficits have been found to persist in children already in remission.

evidence.snippet: with genome-wide linkage of CTS to 11p13 (HLOD 4.30).
evidence.explanation: Maps the centrotemporal-spike EEG trait to the 11p13/ELP4 locus.

genes/0.notes: The heritable centrotemporal-sharp-wave EEG trait maps to the 11p13 locus containing ELP4 (Elongator complex subunit 4); associated variants are largely non-coding/regulatory. This is a susceptibility trait, not a single Mendelian cause; SeLECTS is genetically complex.

evidence.snippet: GRIN2A mutation was found in 11.1% (1 out of 9 cases) of LKS, and in 7.1% (3 out of 42 cases) of ABPE, but in none with ECSWS and BECTS.
evidence.explanation: Shows GRIN2A variants concentrate at the severe end of the spectrum and are absent from classic BECTS/SeLECTS.

genes/1.notes: GRIN2A (encoding the NMDA receptor subunit GluN2A) variants cluster at the severe/atypical end of the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum (Landau-Kleffner syndrome, atypical benign focal epilepsy, EE-SWAS) and are essentially absent from classic SeLECTS/BECTS - a distinction from the GRIN2A monogenic disorders.

evidence.snippet: In most patients with the typical focal idiopathic epilepsy syndromes, medication is not necessary.
evidence.explanation: Supports the "often not required" framing of this treatment.

evidence.snippet: The majority of children had a seizure while being treated with ASMs, suggesting that CECTS is not as pharmacoresponsive as assumed or that treatment approaches are not optimized.
evidence.explanation: Contradicts this treatment's claim that standard antiseizure medications "are effective". In a prospective cohort, 29 of 42 treated children still had seizures on treatment. Recorded as REFUTE rather than dropped, because the description makes an efficacy claim and this is the evidence against it; the "often not required" half is supported separately above.

treatments/0.description: Because seizures are infrequent and self-limited, many children need no antiseizure medication; when treatment is used (e.g., for frequent or daytime seizures), standard focal-epilepsy antiseizure medications are effective.

evidence.snippet: It may be that a syndrome is benign only when it can be recognized early with reasonable certainty, thereby avoiding unnecessary investigations, overtreatment, and lifestyle restrictions.
evidence.explanation: Articulates the rationale for observation and counseling over intervention: early confident recognition is what makes avoiding overtreatment and lifestyle restriction possible.

treatments/1.description: Given the benign, self-limited course, reassurance, family counseling, and observation are often sufficient management.

evidence.snippet: GRIN2A mutation was found in 11.1% (1 out of 9 cases) of LKS, and in 7.1% (3 out of 42 cases) of ABPE, but in none with ECSWS and BECTS.
evidence.explanation: Shows GRIN2A partly explains the severe end but not classic SeLECTS, leaving the determinants of progression largely open.

open_questions/0.rationale: SeLECTS is the mild anchor of a continuum whose severe end carries lasting language and cognitive morbidity. GRIN2A variants are enriched at the severe end and are essentially absent from classic SeLECTS, but they explain only a minority even of severe cases, so the factors (genetic, EEG burden in sleep, others) that tip a given child toward encephalopathic outcome are largely unknown. Because the severe end is where irreversible harm occurs, predicting and preventing progression is the central clinical question of the spectrum.

open_questions/1.rationale: Unlike most epilepsies, SeLECTS is programmed to remit as the brain matures, which makes its offset an unusual natural experiment in how a developing cortical network loses a seizure-generating state. The specific maturational processes (changes in inhibition, myelination, synaptic pruning, or network connectivity of the sensorimotor cortex) responsible for remission are not established. Understanding them could illuminate general principles of epileptogenesis and its reversal.

evidence.snippet: with genome-wide linkage of CTS to 11p13 (HLOD 4.30).
evidence.explanation: Establishes the heritable EEG trait locus whose incomplete penetrance and language pleiotropy are the subject of this hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: Pleiotropic effects of the 11p13 locus on developmental verbal dyspraxia and EEG centrotemporal sharp waves.
evidence.explanation: Ties the same 11p13 locus to both the EEG trait and developmental verbal dyspraxia, the pleiotropy this hypothesis addresses.

open_questions/2.rationale: The CTS EEG trait maps to 11p13/ELP4 and is far more common than clinical SeLECTS, so most trait carriers never have seizures - the determinants of this incomplete, age-dependent penetrance are unknown. The same locus shows pleiotropy with developmental verbal dyspraxia, hinting that the EEG trait and the language phenotype share a developmental substrate. Whether ELP4 regulatory variation sets a cortical-excitability and language-network vulnerability that only sometimes crosses the seizure threshold is an open, testable hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: In this study, we performed whole-exome sequencing in six unrelated probands with developmental delay, macrocephaly, and dysmorphic features. All six had de novo truncating variants in ASXL2.
evidence.explanation: The defining observation: de novo truncating variants in every proband.

evidence.snippet: We were also able to demonstrate with mRNA studies that these variants are likely to exert a dominant-negative effect, given that both alleles are expressed in blood and the mutated ASXL2 transcripts escape nonsense-mediated decay.
evidence.explanation: The mRNA evidence behind the dominant-negative assignment on this node. Note the source's own hedge - "likely to exert" - and the contrary evidence recorded in the discussion below.

steps/1.description:
Heterozygous truncating variants - nonsense and frameshift - in ASXL2. The defining series found six such variants in six unrelated probands, all de novo. Reported alleles since include p.Ser627Phefs*22 and further nonsense changes, and one family reached the same diagnosis through a balanced chromosomal rearrangement disrupting the gene rather than through a point variant.
The variant class matters. All three ASXL germline diseases are caused by truncating variants, not missense, which is the observation the dominant-negative and gain-of-function arguments in this gene family are built on.

evidence.snippet: The ASXL genes (ASXL1, ASXL2, and ASXL3) participate in body patterning during embryogenesis and encode proteins involved in epigenetic regulation and assembly of transcription factors to specific genomic loci.
evidence.explanation: The functional assignment of the gene family.

evidence.snippet: Although Asx is characterized as a catalytic partner for the deubiquitinase Calypso (or BAP1), there are domains of ASXL proteins that are distinct from Asx and the roles and redundancies of ASXL members are not yet well understood.
evidence.explanation: The PR-DUB partnership, together with the explicit limits on how far the Drosophila account transfers - which is why this node is PROVISIONAL.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, it is not yet fully clarified if commonly encountered ASXL1 mutations result in a loss of protein or stable expression of a truncated protein with dominant-negative or gain-of-function properties.
evidence.explanation: Graded NO_EVIDENCE deliberately. The sentence is about ASXL1, not ASXL2, so it does not bear on this node's claim either way; it is cited to record that the mechanism question is open across the whole family rather than only here.

steps/2.description:
ASXL proteins are the mammalian homologs of Drosophila Additional sex combs, which balances trithorax and Polycomb function, and they act as the scaffolding partner of the deubiquitinase BAP1 in the PR-DUB complex. The ASXL genes participate in body patterning during embryogenesis and encode proteins involved in epigenetic regulation and in assembling transcription factors at specific genomic loci.
This node is PROVISIONAL, and the reason is specific rather than routine. No chromatin abnormality has been measured in tissue from a person with Shashi-Pena syndrome. The chromatin account is inherited from what is known about ASXL1 and about the mouse, and a review of the family notes that the domains of ASXL proteins are partly distinct from Asx and that the roles and redundancies of the three members are not well understood - including whether truncating variants give loss of protein or a stable truncated protein with dominant-negative or gain-of-function properties.

evidence.snippet: Although overlapping features with Bohring-Opitz and Bainbridge-Ropers syndromes exist, features that distinguish the ASXL2-associated condition from ASXL1- and ASXL3-related disorders are macrocephaly, absence of growth retardation, and more variability in the degree of intellectual disabilities.
evidence.explanation: The three features that separate this disorder from its paralogous neighbours, and the basis for treating the growth direction as a real signal.

evidence.snippet: This study supports the inclusion of SHAPNS in overgrowth disorders with macrocephaly, suggesting the analysis of the ASXL2 gene even in suspected subjects with normal bone age and confirms dental anomalies as a clinical feature of this syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Argues the overgrowth framing explicitly, from a patient at the mild end of the neurodevelopmental spectrum.

steps/3.description:
The route from a chromatin scaffold to macrocephaly, a specific facial gestalt, dental anomalies and variable intellectual disability is not traced. What can be said is that the phenotype is reproducible enough to be recognised clinically, and that it differs from its two paralogous neighbours in a consistent direction - overgrowth rather than growth restriction.
That direction is itself informative and is the reason this node is worth stating separately from the chromatin node: ASXL1 and ASXL3 truncations restrict growth, ASXL2 truncations do not, and one patient has been reported with marked postnatal overgrowth and only minor neurodevelopmental features, which has led to the suggestion that SHAPNS belongs among the overgrowth disorders with macrocephaly.

evidence.snippet: ASXL2 null mice exhibit glucose intolerance, insulin resistance and lipodystrophy. The regulatory role of ASXL2 in glucose and lipid homeostasis occurs through its interaction with peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ), a gene implicated in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes on genome-wide association studies.
evidence.explanation: The mouse phenotype and the proposed molecular link, which is what made the human prediction.

evidence.snippet: We report the first case of type 2 diabetes in Shashi-Pena syndrome, occurring in an 8-year-old prepubertal boy with no family history.
evidence.explanation: The single human case that meets the mouse prediction.

evidence.snippet: Further reported cases will assist in confirming this association.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own statement that one case does not establish the association, which is why this node is PROVISIONAL. Graded INDIRECT: it is a statement about the strength of the evidence rather than a result.

steps/4.description:
ASXL2 interacts with PPAR-gamma, and ASXL2-null mice are glucose-intolerant, insulin-resistant and lipodystrophic. That is a mouse-derived prediction about a human phenotype, and it is one of the few places in this entry where the prediction has been tested: an 8-year-old prepubertal boy with SHAPNS developed type 2 diabetes with dyslipidemia and fatty infiltration of the liver, in the absence of a family history.
It is graded PROVISIONAL because that is one patient. The source itself asks for further cases before treating the association as established, and the infantile hypoglycemia that is well documented in this syndrome is a different metabolic problem in the opposite direction, not obviously part of the same account.

evidence.snippet: Macrosomia and macrocephaly are also common.
evidence.explanation: Frequency statement from GeneReviews, mapped to FREQUENT.

steps/5.description: Common, and one of the three features that distinguish this disorder from Bohring-Opitz and Bainbridge-Ropers syndrome. Macrosomia is also common, and growth retardation is characteristically absent.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals can have variable developmental delay / intellectual disability, ranging from low-average intellectual abilities to severe intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: The range of developmental outcome, from GeneReviews.

steps/6.description: Variable in a way that is clinically important: outcomes range from low-average intellectual ability to severe intellectual disability, and at least one reported patient has only minor neurodevelopmental features. This variability is itself a distinguishing feature against the ASXL1 and ASXL3 disorders.

evidence.snippet: In addition, the proband had dyslipidemia, and fatty infiltration of the liver with elevated transaminases.
evidence.explanation: The accompanying metabolic findings in the single reported case.

steps/7.description: Reported once, prepubertally, with dyslipidemia and hepatic steatosis. It is here because it was predicted by the mouse before it was seen in a person, not because it is expected in a given patient.

evidence.snippet: ASXL2 is frequently mutated in acute myeloid leukaemia patients with t(8;21).
evidence.explanation: The somatic context of the gene, recorded so the germline/somatic distinction in the notes is anchored.

evidence.snippet: The aim of this study was to uncover the genetic cause of delayed psychomotor development and variable intellectual disability in a proband whose previous genetic analyses, including chromosome microarray and whole exome sequencing, had been negative.
evidence.explanation: The diagnostic point: microarray and exome were both negative in a patient who does have an ASXL2 disruption.

genes/0.notes:
ASXL2 ("ASXL transcriptional regulator 2") is the second of three mammalian Additional sex combs-like genes. Its germline disease is Shashi-Pena syndrome; somatically it is recurrently mutated in acute myeloid leukaemia with t(8;21), and mouse deletion produces a myelodysplastic-syndrome-like disease.
Whether that somatic story implies a cancer risk in Shashi-Pena syndrome is not known and should not be asserted from the gene alone. No malignancy surveillance is recommended in the GeneReviews management section, and no case of myeloid malignancy in a person with SHAPNS is cited in the material reviewed here. The germline and somatic variant classes are also not the same problem: the germline disease is caused by truncating variants predicted to act dominant-negatively, while the mouse cancer model is a deletion.
Diagnostically, the point worth taking from the transmitted-translocation family is that a negative exome does not exclude ASXL2. A balanced rearrangement disrupting the gene was invisible to both chromosomal microarray and whole-exome sequencing and needed long-read sequencing plus RNA-seq to find.

evidence.snippet: Surveillance: At each visit, measure growth parameters; evaluate nutritional status and safety of oral intake; monitor for the following: developmental progress and educational needs; difficulties with attention, anger outbursts, and aggression; signs of ADHD, autism, and anxiety; new manifestations, such as seizures and changes in tone; signs/symptoms of temperature dysregulation; signs/symptoms of sleep apnea; signs of feeding difficulties; development of scoliosis/kyphosis; and signs/symptoms of hypoglycemia.
evidence.explanation: The surveillance schedule verbatim, which is the substance of management in this disorder.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying therapy exists. GeneReviews specifies a surveillance programme rather than a treatment: growth parameters and nutritional status at each visit, developmental and educational progress, attention and aggression, signs of ADHD, autism and anxiety, new seizures or tone change, temperature dysregulation, sleep apnea, feeding, scoliosis or kyphosis, and hypoglycemia. Spine radiographs, DXA in those with fractures, dental and ophthalmology review, blood glucose monitoring and audiology follow as clinically indicated.

evidence.snippet: For infants with hypoglycemia, standard treatment with dextrose and avoidance of fasting is reasonable; octreotide has been used in those with hyperinsulinism.
evidence.explanation: The hypoglycemia management, including the specific agent used for hyperinsulinism.

evidence.snippet: Review of healthy eating habits; surveillance for euglycemia, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and consideration of referral to nutrition for those who develop obesity.
evidence.explanation: The metabolic surveillance in the other direction, which is where the diabetes case and the mouse phenotype land clinically.

treatments/1.description: Standard dextrose treatment and avoidance of fasting for infantile hypoglycemia; octreotide has been used where hyperinsulinism is demonstrated. Given the single reported case of prepubertal type 2 diabetes and the mouse metabolic phenotype, GeneReviews also asks for surveillance for euglycemia, hyperlipidemia and hypertension, and nutrition referral in those who become obese - so the metabolic monitoring here runs in both directions.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of manifestations: Feeding therapy for those with feeding difficulties; consideration of nasogastric or gastrostomy tube placement for those with persistent feeding issues.
evidence.explanation: The feeding intervention as specified in the management section.

treatments/2.description: Feeding therapy, with nasogastric or gastrostomy tube placement considered for persistent difficulty.

open_questions/0.rationale:
Two published observations point in opposite directions and neither has been reconciled.
The dominant-negative argument comes from the defining study: the truncated ASXL2 transcripts escape nonsense-mediated decay and both alleles are expressed in blood, so a stable truncated protein is present and could interfere. The paper's own wording is "likely to exert", not "demonstrated". This entry's genetic_context carries functional_impact_category DOMINANT_NEGATIVE on that basis, which is a choice made with the contrary evidence in view rather than in ignorance of it.
The haploinsufficiency argument comes from the family with a balanced t(2;11) translocation, in whom RNA-seq showed *decreased* average ASXL2 mRNA. Those patients have the same syndrome. If reduced dosage alone produces the phenotype, a stable interfering protein is not needed to explain it.
Both can be partly true - a truncated protein could be dominant-negative while dosage reduction is independently sufficient - but that is a hypothesis, not a finding. The same question is explicitly open for ASXL1, where a review notes it is not clarified whether the common mutations give loss of protein or a stable truncated protein with dominant-negative or gain-of-function properties. Resolving it for ASXL2 would also decide whether an ASXL2 whole-gene deletion should be reported as causing this syndrome.

open_questions/1.rationale:
The Asxl2 mouse exists and is well characterised - for myeloid malignancy. Its published readouts are haematopoietic stem cell self-renewal, histone marks in Lin-cKit+ cells, and survival after transplant. Macrocephaly, craniofacial patterning, cognition and the dental phenotype are not among them.
The genotype mismatch compounds the tissue mismatch. The mouse is a deletion; the human disease is caused by truncating alleles whose transcripts escape nonsense-mediated decay. If the dominant-negative account is right, the mouse is not modelling the human lesion at all, and the negative would be uninformative rather than reassuring.
The one place the mouse has predicted a human finding is metabolic - glucose intolerance and lipodystrophy, met by a single case of prepubertal type 2 diabetes. That is a real success and it is recorded as such on the model link. It does not extend to the neurodevelopmental phenotype, which is the disease's main burden and has no model at all.

evidence.snippet: A pseudogene copy (SBDSP) with 97% nucleotide sequence identity resides in a locally duplicated genomic segment of 305 kb.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the pseudogene whose conversion generates the recurrent SDS alleles.

evidence.snippet: Converted segments consistently included at least one of two pseudogene-like sequence changes that result in protein truncation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes protein truncation as the functional consequence of the converted alleles.

steps/3.description: Gene conversion between SBDS and its 97%-identical neighbouring pseudogene SBDSP1 imports pseudogene-derived sequence changes that truncate the protein, leaving a hypomorphic residue of SBDS activity.

evidence.snippet: We show that the encoded protein associates with rRNA and plays a highly conserved role in the maturation of the 60S ribosomal subunit.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the 60S maturation role that biallelic loss disrupts.

evidence.snippet: DNAJC21 deficiency resulted in cytoplasmic accumulation of the 60S nuclear export factor PA2G4, aberrant ribosome profiles, and increased cell death.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived and knockdown cellular data for the proximal molecular defect.

steps/4.description: DNAJC21 is an rRNA-associated co-chaperone acting at two points of ribosome biogenesis. Biallelic loss corrupts early nuclear rRNA processing as well as the late cytoplasmic maturation of the 60S subunit, and traps the 60S export factor PA2G4 in the cytoplasm.

evidence.snippet: Here, by isolating late cytoplasmic 60S ribosomal subunits from Sbds-deleted mice, we show that SBDS and the GTPase elongation factor-like 1 (EFL1) directly catalyze eIF6 removal in mammalian cells by a mechanism that requires GTP binding and hydrolysis by EFL1 but not phosphorylation of eIF6 Ser 235.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates in Sbds-null mouse ribosomes that SBDS and EFL1 jointly catalyse the eviction step lost in SDS.

steps/5.description: Release of the anti-association factor eIF6 is the last step of cytoplasmic 60S maturation and is catalysed by SBDS together with the GTPase EFL1. Disease variants uncouple EFL1 GTP hydrolysis from eIF6 release, so eIF6 remains bound and the subunit cannot join a 40S partner.

evidence.snippet: 3D protein modeling revealed that the 3 variants affect highly conserved amino acids within the GTPase domain of the protein that are critical for GTP and receptor binding. Indeed, we observed that the GTPase activity of the mutated proteins was impaired.
evidence.explanation: Establishes impaired SRP54 GTPase activity as the proximal molecular defect of this subtype.

steps/6.description: In the SRP54-related form the lesion is not ribosome maturation but the signal recognition particle itself. Missense variants in the SRP54 GTPase domain reduce GTPase activity and impair delivery of nascent secretory and membrane polypeptides, a load the granulopoietic and pancreatic acinar compartments are least able to absorb.

evidence.snippet: SBDS, through direct interaction with EFL1, promotes the release of the eukaryotic initiation factor 6 (eIF6) during ribosome maturation, DNAJC21 stabilizes the 80S ribosome, and SRP54 facilitates protein trafficking.
evidence.explanation: Review statement that the SDS genes converge on ribosome maturation and early protein synthesis.

steps/7.description: The convergent cellular lesion of the SBDS, EFL1 and DNAJC21 forms: mature subunits fail to assemble into translating 80S ribosomes. This is the node at which the otherwise distinct causal genes of nosology group 11 meet.

evidence.snippet: SBDS, through direct interaction with EFL1, promotes the release of the eukaryotic initiation factor 6 (eIF6) during ribosome maturation, DNAJC21 stabilizes the 80S ribosome, and SRP54 facilitates protein trafficking.
evidence.explanation: Review statement that the SDS genes converge on ribosome maturation and early protein synthesis.

steps/8.description: Reduced global protein synthesis, the functional consequence that makes SDS a ribosomopathy and the constraint that selects the somatic clones later in the graph.

evidence.snippet: Here we report that multiple independent somatic hematopoietic clones arise early in life, most commonly harboring heterozygous mutations in EIF6 or TP53.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the existence and genetic identity of the two somatic clone classes.

steps/9.description: Multiple independent somatic clones arise in the SDS marrow from early life, selected by the fitness constraint the germline ribosome defect imposes. The clones are not one population: they split into two mechanistically opposed classes with opposite clinical meaning, modelled here as separate downstream nodes so that the graph cannot be read as "clonal hematopoiesis causes leukemia".

evidence.snippet: EIF6 inactivation mediates a compensatory pathway with limited leukemic potential by ameliorating the underlying SDS ribosome defect and enhancing clone fitness.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the compensatory mechanism and the limited leukemic potential that justifies leaving this node without a malignancy edge.

evidence.snippet: As expected, we observed frequent interstitial deletions of chromosome 20q (8 of 17, 47%) in patients without MN
evidence.explanation: Establishes interstitial del(20q) as frequent, and specifically in patients without myeloid neoplasia, which is what marks it as part of the compensatory rather than the pre-malignant arm.

steps/10.description: Somatic EIF6 inactivation ameliorates the underlying ribosome defect and so enhances clone fitness. It carries limited leukemic potential and is deliberately given no edge to malignant transformation: this arm is a compensatory response, not a step toward leukemia, and an edge here would assert the opposite of what the source reports. EIF6 is inactivated by two distinct genetic routes, and both belong here: point mutation, and interstitial deletion of chromosome 20q, which removes the EIF6 locus and is the commoner of the two. This is why del(20q) in an SDS marrow does not carry the ominous meaning it carries in sporadic myelodysplastic syndrome.

evidence.snippet: TP53 mutations define a maladaptive pathway with enhanced leukemic potential by inactivating tumor suppressor checkpoints without correcting the ribosome defect.
evidence.explanation: Establishes this arm as the pre-malignant one.

steps/11.description: Somatic TP53 mutation improves clone fitness by inactivating tumour-suppressor checkpoints while leaving the ribosome defect uncorrected. This is the arm that carries leukemic potential, and progression to overt leukemia is associated with acquisition of biallelic TP53 alterations.

evidence.snippet: several studies have shown that, with advancing age, about 40-60% of patients become pancreatic sufficient
evidence.explanation: Documents the age-dependent partial recovery of exocrine function that distinguishes this node from a fixed structural lesion.

steps/12.description: Acinar tissue is replaced by fat, producing pancreatic enzyme deficiency, steatorrhoea and malabsorption. Unusually for a structural pancreatic disease, secretory capacity often improves with age, and a substantial minority of patients become pancreatic sufficient in later childhood.

evidence.snippet: Intermittent neutropenia is the most common haematological finding in SDS, but more of the bone marrow cellular elements can be involved.
evidence.explanation: Supports both the granulocytic predominance and the broader marrow involvement described in this node.

steps/13.description: Persistent or intermittent neutropenia is the earliest and most constant haematological finding, but the marrow defect is not lineage-restricted and single- or multilineage cytopenias develop over time.

evidence.snippet: Increased apoptosis was observed in SDS-derived BM in combination with p53 overexpression.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the apoptosis and its association with p53 in patient marrow.

evidence.snippet: Loss of SBDS was associated with increased apoptosis when checkpoint pathways were intact but resulted in aneuploid cells when p53 was inactivated.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the two-way dependence on p53 that links the cytopenias to the same checkpoint whose somatic loss drives the maladaptive clonal arm.

steps/14.description: Ribosomal stress activates p53 in haematopoietic progenitors, and the apoptosis that follows is what depletes the marrow. The checkpoint cuts both ways: with p53 intact the cells die, producing the cytopenias, while p53 inactivation lets them survive as aneuploid cells - which is the same checkpoint whose somatic loss defines the pre-malignant clonal arm of this disease.

evidence.snippet: The typical features were (1) delayed appearance of secondary ossification centers, (2) variable widening and irregularity of the metaphyses in early childhood, followed by progressive thickening and irregularity of the growth plates, and (3) generalized osteopenia.
evidence.explanation: Radiographic series in molecularly confirmed patients defining the skeletal lesion of this node.

steps/15.description: The skeletal arm of the disease. Radiographs show delayed appearance of secondary ossification centres, then widening and irregularity of the metaphyses that progresses with age, together with generalised osteopenia. The metaphyseal component worsens while the epiphyseal maturation delay tends to normalise, which is why the nosology classifies SDS as a metaphyseal rather than an epiphyseal dysplasia.

evidence.snippet: Short ribs with broadened anterior ends and metaphyseal dyschondroplasia of the long bone are the most common findings.
evidence.explanation: Names the two commonest radiographic findings that constitute this node.

steps/16.description: The clinically expressed skeletal lesion: metaphyseal dyschondroplasia of the long bones, short ribs with broadened anterior ends, and thoracic narrowing.

evidence.snippet: exocrine pancreatic dysfunction with malabsorption, malnutrition, and growth failure
evidence.explanation: States the pancreatic-to-malnutrition step directly.

steps/17.description: Fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption secondary to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. This is the nutritional route to poor growth, distinct from the skeletal one.

evidence.snippet: In almost all affected children, persistent or intermittent neutropenia is an early finding. Short stature and recurrent infections are common.
evidence.explanation: Records short stature as a common manifestation.

steps/18.description: Short stature in SDS has two converging causes, modelled here as two incoming edges: the intrinsic skeletal growth defect, and malnutrition from exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Studies indicating that patients are genuinely short rather than merely undernourished are why the skeletal route is drawn at all.

evidence.snippet: In almost all affected children, persistent or intermittent neutropenia is an early finding. Short stature and recurrent infections are common.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews records recurrent infection as a common manifestation alongside the early neutropenia.

steps/19.description: Recurrent bacterial infection, particularly respiratory and otologic, is a common presenting problem and the main indication for G-CSF.

evidence.snippet: In 10-30% of cases, transformation to a myeloid neoplasm occurs.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the transformation risk described in this node.

evidence.snippet: Increased risk of hematologic malignancies at young ages and the rarity of solid malignancies was observed in both the NCI cohort and published studies.
evidence.explanation: Cohort evidence for the young age at malignancy and the restriction to haematological cancers.

steps/20.description: Progression to myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia occurs in a substantial minority of patients, typically at a young age, and is the principal determinant of prognosis. Solid tumours are rare.

evidence.snippet: Most patients had the SDS hallmark features of neutropenia (45/45, 100%), pancreatic insufficiency (41/43, 95.3%), and/or bony abnormalities (29/36, 80.6%).
evidence.explanation: NCI cohort frequency for neutropenia in molecularly characterised SDS.

steps/21.description: Persistent or intermittent neutropenia, present in essentially all affected children and usually the earliest abnormality.

evidence.snippet: Neutrophils isolated from SDS patients exhibit dysregulated chemotaxis due to altered F-actin polymerization capability.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived neutrophils establish the chemotaxis defect and its cytoskeletal basis.

evidence.snippet: Attenuated chemotaxis in neutrophil was shown in a srp54 knockdown zebrafish model.
evidence.explanation: Model-organism confirmation of the same functional defect in the SRP54 form.

steps/22.description: A functional neutrophil defect distinct from, and additional to, the low neutrophil count: SDS neutrophils show dysregulated chemotaxis traced to altered F-actin polymerization. It matters clinically because it means infection risk is not fully predicted by the absolute neutrophil count, and it is reproduced in the srp54 zebrafish model.

evidence.snippet: Most patients had the SDS hallmark features of neutropenia (45/45, 100%), pancreatic insufficiency (41/43, 95.3%), and/or bony abnormalities (29/36, 80.6%).
evidence.explanation: Same cohort provides the frequency of pancreatic insufficiency.

steps/23.description: Fatty replacement of the pancreas with enzyme deficiency, steatorrhoea and malabsorption; present in over 95% of cohort patients, though secretory capacity may improve with age.

evidence.snippet: Short ribs with broadened anterior ends and metaphyseal dyschondroplasia of the long bone are the most common findings.
evidence.explanation: Identifies metaphyseal dyschondroplasia as one of the two commonest skeletal findings.

evidence.snippet: There was a tendency towards normalization of the epiphyseal maturation defect and progression of the metaphyseal changes with age.
evidence.explanation: Supports the progressive clinical course annotated on this phenotype.

steps/24.description: Metaphyseal dyschondroplasia of the long bones with widening and irregularity that progresses through childhood; the feature that places SDS in the metaphyseal group of the ISDS skeletal nosology.

evidence.snippet: The typical features were (1) delayed appearance of secondary ossification centers, (2) variable widening and irregularity of the metaphyses in early childhood, followed by progressive thickening and irregularity of the growth plates, and (3) generalized osteopenia.
evidence.explanation: Lists generalised osteopenia among the typical radiographic features.

steps/25.description: Generalised osteopenia is a consistent radiographic finding across the SDS skeletal series.

evidence.snippet: Short ribs with broadened anterior ends and metaphyseal dyschondroplasia of the long bone are the most common findings.
evidence.explanation: The rib abnormality underlying the narrow thorax is named as one of the commonest findings.

steps/26.description: Short ribs with broadened anterior ends narrow the thorax; severe thoracic dystrophy is the reason GeneReviews recommends early pulmonary and orthopaedic referral.

evidence.snippet: In almost all affected children, persistent or intermittent neutropenia is an early finding. Short stature and recurrent infections are common.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews records short stature as a common manifestation.

steps/27.description: Short stature reflects an intrinsic growth defect as well as malabsorption; weight and length are deficient from birth and remain below normal.

evidence.snippet: All patients present features consistent with IBMFS: bone marrow failure, growth retardation, failure to thrive, developmental delay, recurrent infections, and skin, teeth or hair abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Documents failure to thrive in the DNAJC21-related form of the spectrum.

steps/28.description: Malabsorption from exocrine pancreatic insufficiency causes failure to thrive, often the presenting complaint in infancy.

evidence.snippet: Patients with SDS often experience recurrent infections due to neutropenia and in some patients hypogammaglobulinemia.
evidence.explanation: Supports recurrent infection as a consequence of the immune defect.

steps/29.description: Neutropenia, sometimes with hypogammaglobulinaemia, causes recurrent bacterial infection.

evidence.snippet: Almost 15-20% of patients with SDS present myelodysplastic syndrome with a high risk of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) transformation.
evidence.explanation: Gives the reported frequency of MDS and its onward leukemic risk.

steps/30.description: Myelodysplastic syndrome develops in a substantial minority and marks the transition from marrow failure to clonal disease.

evidence.snippet: In 10-30% of cases, transformation to a myeloid neoplasm occurs.
evidence.explanation: Reports the frequency of transformation to myeloid neoplasia including AML.

steps/31.description: AML is the principal malignant outcome, arises at young ages, and is associated with acquisition of biallelic TP53 alterations in the marrow.

evidence.snippet: hematologic abnormalities with single- or multilineage cytopenias and susceptibility to myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myelogenous leukemia (AML)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents multilineage cytopenia as part of the haematological phenotype.

steps/32.description: Marrow involvement is not confined to the granulocytic lineage; single- or multilineage cytopenias develop and may progress to severe marrow failure.

evidence.snippet: Developmental delay was common (20/34, 58.8%).
evidence.explanation: Cohort frequency for developmental delay.

steps/33.description: Developmental delay and attention or learning problems are common and increasingly recognised as part of the phenotype rather than a consequence of chronic illness.

evidence.snippet: Elevated liver enzymes and hepatomegaly are present in the first years of life with subsequent improvement without complications.
evidence.explanation: Supports both the finding and the transient course annotated here.

steps/34.description: Transient hepatomegaly with elevated liver enzymes is typical in the first years of life and usually improves without sequelae.

evidence.snippet: Both cases had neonatal skeletal manifestations that included platyspondyly, lacy iliac crests and severe metaphysial dysplasia, and thus did not fall in the range of the known Shwachman-Diamond syndrome skeletal phenotype but resembled spondylometaphysial dysplasia (SMD) Sedaghatian type.
evidence.explanation: Names platyspondyly as a neonatal skeletal manifestation in both reported patients.

steps/35.description: Flattening of the vertebral bodies, present in the newborn period. This is the finding that makes the severe neonatal form spondylometaphyseal; the classic SDS skeleton is metaphyseal with delayed epiphyseal ossification and is not platyspondylic.

evidence.snippet: A British boy was a stillbirth with pulmonary hypoplasia and hepatic fibrosis found on autopsy.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy source for pulmonary hypoplasia in the stillborn patient.

steps/36.description: Underdeveloped lungs, found at autopsy in the stillborn patient of this subtype.

evidence.snippet: An 11-year-old Japanese girl presented with neonatal respiratory failure necessitating lifelong ventilation support, severe short stature and severe developmental delay.
evidence.explanation: Reports the neonatal onset and the lifelong ventilator dependence recorded here, in the surviving patient.

steps/37.description: Respiratory failure from the neonatal period onward, severe enough to require permanent ventilatory support in the one patient of this subtype who survived the newborn period.

evidence.snippet: A British boy was a stillbirth with pulmonary hypoplasia and hepatic fibrosis found on autopsy.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy source for hepatic fibrosis in the stillborn patient.

steps/38.description: Established liver fibrosis at autopsy in the stillborn patient. This is a different hepatic lesion from the transient transaminase elevation of classic SDS, which resolves without sequelae.

evidence.snippet: Functional analysis of disease-associated missense variants reveals that the essential role of SBDS is to tightly couple GTP hydrolysis by EFL1 on the ribosome to eIF6 release.
evidence.explanation: Directly attributes the eviction failure to loss of SBDS function.

edges/3.description: SBDS is the cofactor that couples EFL1 GTP hydrolysis to eIF6 release, so its loss blocks the eviction step directly.

evidence.snippet: DNAJC21 deficiency resulted in cytoplasmic accumulation of the 60S nuclear export factor PA2G4, aberrant ribosome profiles, and increased cell death.
evidence.explanation: Cellular data showing aberrant ribosome profiles, the direct in-vitro support for this edge. The paper's combined causality conclusion is cited instead in the genetic section, where its human-genetic character is the point.

edges/4.description: Corrupted 60S maturation reduces the pool of subunits competent to form translating 80S ribosomes.

evidence.snippet: Our findings establish a direct role for SBDS and EFL1 in catalyzing the translational activation of ribosomes in all eukaryotes, and define SDS as a ribosomopathy caused by uncoupling GTP hydrolysis from eIF6 release.
evidence.explanation: States that the eviction defect is what withholds translational activation of the ribosome.

edges/5.description: eIF6 retained on the 60S subunit sterically blocks subunit joining, so fewer 80S ribosomes are formed.

evidence.snippet: Profound reductions in neutrophil counts and chemotaxis as well as a diminished exocrine pancreas size in a SRP54-knockdown zebrafish model faithfully recapitulated the human phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Model-organism evidence linking loss of SRP54 function to the granulopoietic and pancreatic phenotype.

edges/6.description: Zebrafish knockdown of SRP54 reproduces the neutrophil deficit and chemotaxis defect seen in patients.

evidence.snippet: Profound reductions in neutrophil counts and chemotaxis as well as a diminished exocrine pancreas size in a SRP54-knockdown zebrafish model faithfully recapitulated the human phenotype.
evidence.explanation: The pancreatic component of the same model-organism result.

edges/7.description: The same knockdown reduces exocrine pancreas size, matching the pancreatic arm of the human phenotype.

evidence.snippet: SBDS, through direct interaction with EFL1, promotes the release of the eukaryotic initiation factor 6 (eIF6) during ribosome maturation, DNAJC21 stabilizes the 80S ribosome, and SRP54 facilitates protein trafficking.
evidence.explanation: Places the SDS genes at ribosome maturation, upstream of the protein synthesis this edge lowers.

edges/8.description: Fewer competent 80S ribosomes lowers global protein synthesis. The two steps are close together in time but are separate claims: a cell could in principle compensate for reduced assembly, and the somatic EIF6 arm of this disease is precisely such a compensation.

edges/9.description: A functional neutrophil defect independent of the count, so patients can be infection-prone at numbers that look adequate. Drawn from the translation deficit rather than from the marrow node because it is a defect of the cells produced, not of their production.

edges/10.description: Neurodevelopmental involvement, reported in a subset. No cited source traces a route from the translation deficit to it.

edges/11.description: Hepatic involvement, which in this disease is usually transient in early childhood.

edges/12.description: The biochemical correlate of that hepatic involvement, and usually the way it is detected.

evidence.snippet: Archaeal orthologs are located within highly conserved operons that include homologs of RNA-processing genes, suggesting that SDS may be caused by a deficiency in an aspect of RNA metabolism that is essential for development of the exocrine pancreas, hematopoiesis and chrondrogenesis.
evidence.explanation: A hedged inference in the 2003 discovery paper, from archaeal operon synteny rather than functional work, that the RNA/ribosome defect selects this tissue. Consistent with the edge but not establishing it, hence partial support.

edges/13.description: The acinar cell, among the most secretory in the body, is disproportionately sensitive to a global translation deficit.

evidence.snippet: Archaeal orthologs are located within highly conserved operons that include homologs of RNA-processing genes, suggesting that SDS may be caused by a deficiency in an aspect of RNA metabolism that is essential for development of the exocrine pancreas, hematopoiesis and chrondrogenesis.
evidence.explanation: A hedged inference in the 2003 discovery paper, from archaeal operon synteny rather than functional work, that the RNA/ribosome defect selects this tissue. Consistent with the edge but not establishing it, hence partial support.

edges/14.description: Hematopoietic progenitors, and the granulocytic lineage in particular, cannot sustain output under the translation deficit.

evidence.snippet: Archaeal orthologs are located within highly conserved operons that include homologs of RNA-processing genes, suggesting that SDS may be caused by a deficiency in an aspect of RNA metabolism that is essential for development of the exocrine pancreas, hematopoiesis and chrondrogenesis.
evidence.explanation: A hedged inference in the 2003 discovery paper, from archaeal operon synteny rather than functional work, that the RNA/ribosome defect selects this tissue. Consistent with the edge but not establishing it, hence partial support.

edges/15.description: Chondrogenesis is the third tissue named as sensitive to the SDS defect, and is the origin of the metaphyseal dysplasia that places SDS in the metaphyseal group of the skeletal nosology.

evidence.snippet: We show that germline SBDS deficiency establishes a fitness constraint that drives selection of somatic clones via two distinct mechanisms with different clinical consequences.
evidence.explanation: Longitudinal patient sequencing links the germline ribosome defect to clonal selection in the marrow.

edges/16.description: The translation deficit is itself the selective pressure: it constrains hematopoietic clone fitness and thereby selects somatic mutants.

edges/17.description: The clinical diagnosis this node describes: acinar loss and fatty replacement leave too little enzyme output to digest fat.

edges/18.description: Malabsorption from that enzyme deficiency is the usual route to infantile growth failure here, and the reason pancreatic enzyme replacement is first-line.

evidence.snippet: exocrine pancreatic dysfunction with malabsorption, malnutrition, and growth failure
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states the causal sequence from pancreatic dysfunction to growth failure.

edges/19.description: Fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption drive failure to thrive.

edges/20.description: The predominant and often earliest cytopenia — this is the finding that places the disease in the IUIS phagocyte table.

edges/21.description: Progression to multilineage failure, in a minority but a clinically decisive one.

edges/22.description: The infectious consequence of the neutropenia, and the commonest infection pattern in this disease.

evidence.snippet: Increased apoptosis was observed in SDS-derived BM in combination with p53 overexpression.
evidence.explanation: Patient marrow shows increased apoptosis together with p53 overexpression, the observation this edge rests on.

edges/23.description: Ribosomal stress from the maturation defect activates p53 in marrow progenitors, and the resulting apoptosis is the proximate reason the cytopenias develop.

evidence.snippet: Patients with SDS often experience recurrent infections due to neutropenia and in some patients hypogammaglobulinemia.
evidence.explanation: Directly states the causal link from neutropenia to recurrent infection in an SDS cohort.

edges/24.description: Neutropenia, compounded in some patients by hypogammaglobulinaemia, predisposes to recurrent bacterial infection.

evidence.snippet: There was a tendency towards normalization of the epiphyseal maturation defect and progression of the metaphyseal changes with age.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the metaphyseal lesion as the progressive component driving the clinical dysplasia.

edges/25.description: Disordered metaphyseal growth produces the clinical skeletal dysplasia and contributes to short stature independently of malnutrition.

evidence.snippet: Both cases had neonatal skeletal manifestations that included platyspondyly, lacy iliac crests and severe metaphysial dysplasia, and thus did not fall in the range of the known Shwachman-Diamond syndrome skeletal phenotype but resembled spondylometaphysial dysplasia (SMD) Sedaghatian type.
evidence.explanation: Reports platyspondyly together with the metaphyseal lesion in both patients. The shared vertebral-endplate growth plate is the inferred substrate, not a claim the source makes, so the item is graded INDIRECT.

edges/26.description: In the severe neonatal presentation the growth-plate lesion also involves the vertebral endplate physes, so the vertebral bodies are already flattened at birth and the dysplasia reads as spondylometaphyseal rather than purely metaphyseal.

edges/27.description: The clinical and radiographic finding this node describes. Note the entry carries a pathophysiology node and a phenotype whose names differ only in casing; they are separate objects and the graph matches names exactly, so this edge connects the two rather than collapsing them.

edges/28.description: Thoracic involvement of the same skeletal dysplasia — the rib-cage expression, which at its most severe restricts lung growth.

edges/29.description: Reduced bone density accompanying the dysplasia.

evidence.snippet: In almost all affected children, persistent or intermittent neutropenia is an early finding. Short stature and recurrent infections are common.
evidence.explanation: Establishes short stature as a common outcome in a disease whose skeletal lesion is described in the preceding node.

edges/30.description: Disordered metaphyseal growth contributes to short stature independently of the nutritional route.

edges/31.description: The clinical finding this node describes; the same name-casing distinction as above applies.

evidence.snippet: Growth retardation is a typical manifestation.
evidence.explanation: Confirms growth failure as a typical manifestation of the disease.

edges/32.description: Malnutrition compounds the intrinsic skeletal growth defect, the second of the two routes into short stature.

evidence.snippet: EIF6 inactivation mediates a compensatory pathway with limited leukemic potential by ameliorating the underlying SDS ribosome defect and enhancing clone fitness.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the compensatory clonal pathway and its limited leukemic potential.

edges/33.description: The compensatory arm, selected because inactivating EIF6 partially corrects the very defect that constrains clone fitness.

evidence.snippet: TP53 mutations define a maladaptive pathway with enhanced leukemic potential by inactivating tumor suppressor checkpoints without correcting the ribosome defect.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the maladaptive clonal pathway and its enhanced leukemic potential.

edges/34.description: The pre-malignant arm, selected by removing tumour-suppressor checkpoints rather than by correcting the ribosome defect.

evidence.snippet: Subsequent development of leukemia was associated with acquisition of biallelic TP53 alterations.
evidence.explanation: Ties the transition to overt leukemia to biallelic TP53 inactivation rather than to clonal hematopoiesis as such.

edges/35.description: Progression to overt myeloid malignancy follows acquisition of biallelic TP53 alterations within this clonal lineage.

edges/36.description: The usual first step of transformation, and what surveillance marrow examination is looking for.

edges/37.description: Frank leukaemia, the endpoint that dominates long-term prognosis and the reason clonal surveillance matters in this disease.

edges/38.description: A severely narrow thorax restricts fetal and infant lung growth. This is the severe end of the skeletal phenotype and the route by which a bone dysplasia becomes lethal.

edges/39.description: The consequence of hypoplastic lungs in the neonatal period, and the reason the thoracic form of this dysplasia carries a different prognosis from the limb form.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report identification of disease-associated mutations in an uncharacterized gene, SBDS, in the interval of 1.9 cM at 7q11 previously shown to be associated with the disease.
evidence.explanation: The original identification of SBDS as the SDS disease gene.

evidence.snippet: Approximately 90% of patients have biallelic pathogenic variants in the SBDS gene located on human chromosome 7q11.
evidence.explanation: Source for the case fraction recorded here.

genes/0.notes: Most alleles arise by gene conversion with the SBDSP1 pseudogene, producing the recurrent c.258+2T>C and c.183_184TA>CT changes. Biallelic null genotypes are not observed, implying residual function is required for life.

evidence.snippet: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that mutations in DNAJC21 cause a cancer-prone BMF syndrome due to corruption of early nuclear rRNA biogenesis and late cytoplasmic maturation of the 60S subunit.
evidence.explanation: Establishes causality and the molecular mechanism for this gene.

genes/1.notes: Biallelic variants cause a cancer-prone bone marrow failure syndrome through corruption of nuclear rRNA biogenesis and late cytoplasmic 60S maturation.

evidence.snippet: In conclusion, autosomal dominant mutations in SRP54, a key member of the cotranslation protein-targeting pathway, lead to syndromic neutropenia with a Shwachman-Diamond-like phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Establishes SRP54 as a dominant cause within the SDS spectrum.

evidence.snippet: To date, SBDS, DNAJC21, and SRP54 variants have been associated with myeloid neoplasia.
evidence.explanation: Records that the SRP54 form shares the myeloid-neoplasia risk.

genes/2.notes: Heterozygous, usually de novo, missense variants in the GTPase domain. Reported alongside SBDS and DNAJC21 as an SDS gene associated with myeloid neoplasia.

evidence.snippet: Autosomal recessive SDS: SDS caused by pathogenic variants in DNAJC21, EFL1, or SBDS is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists EFL1 among the recessive SDS genes.

genes/3.notes: The fourth SDS gene, curated in full in the separate EFL1-related Shwachman-Diamond syndrome entry; listed here so the genetic spectrum of the disease is complete.

evidence.snippet: Subsequent development of leukemia was associated with acquisition of biallelic TP53 alterations.
evidence.explanation: Links somatic biallelic TP53 loss to leukemic progression in SDS.

genes/4.notes: Not a germline cause. Somatic TP53 mutation is the maladaptive clonal pathway in the SDS marrow, and biallelic TP53 loss accompanies progression to leukemia.

evidence.snippet: EIF6 inactivation mediates a compensatory pathway with limited leukemic potential by ameliorating the underlying SDS ribosome defect and enhancing clone fitness.
evidence.explanation: Establishes somatic EIF6 loss as a compensatory rather than pre-malignant event.

genes/5.notes: Somatic EIF6 inactivation partially corrects the germline ribosome defect and expands clones with limited leukemic potential; the mechanistic mirror image of the TP53 pathway and a candidate therapeutic target.

evidence.snippet: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is treated with oral pancreatic enzymes and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation.
evidence.explanation: Standard-of-care statement for the pancreatic component.

treatments/0.description: Oral pancreatic enzymes with fat-soluble vitamin supplementation are the standard treatment for the exocrine pancreatic component.

evidence.snippet: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is treated with oral pancreatic enzymes and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews names enzyme replacement as the treatment aimed at this mechanism.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replaces the enzymatic output the failing acinar tissue cannot provide; it does not correct the underlying ribosomal defect.

evidence.snippet: Prolonged use of cytokine and hematopoietic growth factors (e.g., G-CSF) should be considered with caution.
evidence.explanation: Records the caution that qualifies this treatment in a leukemia-predisposition syndrome.

treatments/1.description: G-CSF is considered for severe recurrent infection with an absolute neutrophil count persistently at or below 500/mm3, and is particularly useful as cover for dental or orthopaedic procedures. Prolonged use is approached with caution given the underlying leukemia predisposition.

evidence.snippet: If recurrent infections are severe and absolute neutrophil counts are persistently ≤500/mm3, treatment with granulocyte-colony stimulation factor (G-CSF) can be considered and may be especially helpful when interventions such as complex dental procedures or orthopedic surgery are being considered.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews indication statement for G-CSF in SDS.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Drives residual granulopoiesis to raise the neutrophil count without addressing the ribosome defect that constrains it.

evidence.snippet: Some drugs used in standard HSCT preparative regimens (e.g., cyclophosphamide and busulfan) may not be suitable because of possible cardiac toxicity.
evidence.explanation: Documents the SDS-specific conditioning caveat.

treatments/2.description: HSCT is the only curative option for the haematological disease and is considered for severe marrow failure, MDS or AML. Conditioning is modified because standard agents such as cyclophosphamide and busulfan carry a risk of cardiac toxicity in SDS.

evidence.snippet: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) should be considered for treatment of severe bone marrow failure, MDS, or AML.
evidence.explanation: Standard-of-care statement for transplantation in SDS marrow disease.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Replaces the SBDS-deficient haematopoietic compartment with donor cells, correcting the marrow arm of the disease while leaving the pancreatic and skeletal arms untouched.

evidence.snippet: Blood and/or platelet transfusions may be considered for anemia and thrombocytopenia.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management statement for the cytopenias.

treatments/3.description: Transfusion support is used for symptomatic anaemia and thrombocytopenia arising from marrow failure.

evidence.snippet: Monitor for orthopedic complications with radiographs of the hips and knees during the most rapid growth stages.
evidence.explanation: Surveillance recommendation supporting ongoing orthopaedic follow-up.

treatments/4.description: Early orthopaedic and pulmonary referral is required for thoracic dystrophy; skeletal dysplasia, asymmetric growth and joint deformities need ongoing orthopaedic management, with hip and knee radiographs during rapid growth.

evidence.snippet: Early pulmonary and orthopedic referral is essential for treatment of thoracic dystrophy; orthopedic management of other skeletal manifestations including skeletal dysplasia, asymmetric growth, and joint deformities.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management statement for the skeletal manifestations.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Manages the mechanical consequences of disordered metaphyseal growth rather than the growth-plate lesion itself.

evidence.snippet: Assessment of nutritional status and measurement of serum concentration of fat-soluble vitamins every six months.
evidence.explanation: Surveillance recommendation for the nutritional consequences of the disease.

treatments/5.description: Nutritional status and fat-soluble vitamin concentrations are followed every six months because malabsorption persists even on enzyme replacement.

evidence.snippet: The observation of biallelic null mutations in four of eight families indicated that the SPENCD phenotype results from a loss of TRAP activity.
evidence.explanation: Null alleles in half the founding families identify loss of TRAP activity, not a neomorphic effect, as the initiating lesion.

steps/1.description: Homozygous or compound heterozygous ACP5 alleles — missense, nonsense, frameshift, or whole-gene deletion — remove functional tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase. Missense alleles are not partial: they are expressed but catalytically inactive, so the initiating lesion is the same across the allelic spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Type-5 acid phosphatase, also known as tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP), is a lysosomal hydrolase expressed in cells of monocytic lineage, with activity against a wide variety of substrates
evidence.explanation: Establishes the enzyme's cellular distribution, which is what makes a bone enzyme deficiency an immune disease.

evidence.snippet: Compared to five age-matched controls, and an unaffected sibling to patients 2 and 3 who was homozygous for the wild-type allele on gene sequencing, levels of total TRAP protein were negligible, and TRAP 5a protein undetectable, indicating an almost complete lack of TRAP synthesis or secretion in the affected patients tested
evidence.explanation: Direct patient measurement establishing that the disease state is absence of TRAP protein.

evidence.snippet: levels of total TRAP protein were negligible, and TRAP 5a protein undetectable, indicating an almost complete lack of TRAP synthesis or secretion in the affected patients tested
evidence.explanation: Protein-level measurement in patient plasma confirms near-complete absence of the enzyme.

steps/2.description: TRAP is a di-iron purple acid phosphatase with a low pH optimum, expressed by osteoclasts, macrophages, and dendritic cells. Its activity is undetectable in patient serum and leukocyte homogenates and roughly halved in heterozygous parents. This node is the point at which the skeletal and immune arms of the disorder diverge.

evidence.snippet: These mutations result in the loss of regulation of TRAP activity on the function of osteopontin (OPN), leading to an excess of phosphorylated OPN.
evidence.explanation: States the substrate-accumulation step as the accepted proximate consequence of TRAP loss.

steps/3.description: Osteopontin accumulates in its hyperphosphorylated form. Dephosphorylation of osteopontin by TRAP is required for osteoclast migration, and intracellular phosphorylated osteopontin has been proposed to couple the TLR9/MyD88 signalosome to interferon-alpha expression in plasmacytoid dendritic cells.

evidence.snippet: CpG-A stimulation in a pDC line with stable knockdown of TRAP resulted in increased expression of IFN
evidence.explanation: A TRAP-knockdown plasmacytoid dendritic cell line responds to TLR9 ligand with excess interferon, the cell-level basis for this node.

steps/4.description: Knockdown of TRAP in a plasmacytoid dendritic cell line raises interferon-alpha protein, interferon-stimulated gene expression, and IRF7 nuclear translocation on CpG-A stimulation, the in vitro correlate of unrestrained TLR9 signalling.

evidence.snippet: Acp5-null mice are viable under laboratory conditions but suffer from developmental deformities of the limb and axial skeleton
evidence.explanation: The null mouse establishes that loss of TRAP is sufficient for a skeletal dysplasia independent of any immune phenotype.

steps/5.description: TRAP loss impairs osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and disorders the endochondral growth plate. In the Acp5-null mouse this produces mild osteopetrosis with disorganised growth plates and bones that are stronger, not weaker, than wild type — consistent with the absence of increased fracture risk in SPENCD.

evidence.snippet: The characteristic skeletal radiological features of SPENCD are (1) platyspondyly, with irregularity of both upper and lower end plates and nodular lesions particularly involving the posterior aspect of the vertebral bodies
evidence.explanation: Defines the vertebral component of the radiographic phenotype.

steps/6.description: The radiographic core of the disorder: platyspondyly with irregular upper and lower vertebral end plates and posterior nodular lesions, together with radiolucent punched-out non-ossifying lesions running from the growth plate into the metaphysis and diaphysis, typically at the distal femur, proximal fibula, and distal radius and ulna.

evidence.snippet: All eight cases assayed showed elevated serum interferon alpha activity, and gene expression profiling in whole blood defined a type I interferon signature.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the elevated interferon activity and the transcriptional signature in patients.

evidence.snippet: Type I IFN signalling is enhanced in the majority of patients tested, although whether this is a driver of pathology or simply represents a disease biomarker remains unclear.
evidence.explanation: Records that the causal status of the interferon signature is itself an open question, which is why downstream edges from this node are hedged.

steps/7.description: Serum interferon-alpha activity is elevated and whole blood carries an interferon-stimulated gene signature in the great majority of patients tested, persisting across repeat measurements. This is the finding that classified SPENCD as a type I interferonopathy. Whether it drives the pathology or is a biomarker of it is not settled.

evidence.snippet: Of particular note was the diverse spectrum of autoimmune phenotypes observed in these individuals (cases), including systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren's syndrome, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, hypothyroidism, inflammatory myositis, Raynaud's disease and vitiligo.
evidence.explanation: Source for the breadth of the autoimmune spectrum described here.

evidence.snippet: at least one autoimmune diagnosis was recorded in 22 patients overall (85%), with 9 (34%) assigned 3 or more such diagnoses
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the autoimmune burden in the best-characterised cohort.

evidence.snippet: Patients showed elevated inflammatory activity, with enrichment of the NF-κB, MAPK, and cell death pathways, as well as up-regulation of type I interferon (IFN) genes in monocytes.
evidence.explanation: The 2026 multicentre cohort adds transcriptomic confirmation of elevated inflammatory activity; the same sentence names NF-kappaB, MAPK, and cell-death pathway enrichment alongside the interferon signature.

steps/8.description: At least one autoimmune diagnosis is recorded in the large majority of patients, and a third carry three or more. Immune thrombocytopenia, systemic lupus erythematosus, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, and hypothyroidism are the commonest; antinuclear and anti-dsDNA antibodies are near-universal. The thrombocytopenia is characteristically treatment-refractory and has caused death and intracranial haemorrhage.

evidence.snippet: Such variable phenotypic presentations were masking the disease and led to the delay in diagnosis until exome sequencing was used revealing homozygous variants in the ACP5 gene as the cause of the patients' phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Documents the diagnostic delay caused by a neurology-dominant presentation.

evidence.snippet: observed spasticity in 11 patients (44%), and intracranial calcification on computed tomography imaging in 9 of 13 patients assessed, variably involving the basal ganglia, pons, cerebellar dentate nuclei, and white-grey matter junction
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency and anatomical distribution of the two neurological features.

steps/9.description: Spasticity, sometimes evident in the first months of life, with calcification of the basal ganglia and other sites on computed tomography, and learning difficulty in a minority. Unlike Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome, significant cerebral white matter disease is unusual.

evidence.snippet: In 1976, Schorr, Legum, and Oshchorn described two brothers with a skeletal dysplasia notable for the presence of flattened vertebrae (platyspondyly) and islands of chondroid tissue within bone (enchondroma), a combination leading them to coin the novel term spondyloenchondrodysplasia (SPENCD)
evidence.explanation: The naming account, which records platyspondyly as one of the two defining radiographic findings.

evidence.snippet: The characteristic skeletal radiological features of SPENCD are (1) platyspondyly, with irregularity of both upper and lower end plates and nodular lesions particularly involving the posterior aspect of the vertebral bodies
evidence.explanation: Names platyspondyly as a characteristic radiological feature.

evidence.snippet: X-Ray of spine showed platyspondyly and X-Ray of forearm and wrist showed metaphyseal dysplasia
evidence.explanation: Documents platyspondyly on plain radiography in a molecularly confirmed patient.

steps/10.description: Flattened vertebral bodies with irregular upper and lower end plates and nodular lesions on the posterior aspect. Present from infancy and one of the two radiographic features that define the disorder.

evidence.snippet: Radiological investigations in our patients revealed the characteristic metaphyseal and vertebral bone lesions described in SPENCD.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the metaphyseal lesions in the founding molecularly defined cohort.

steps/11.description: Radiolucent, punched-out non-ossifying lesions extending from the growth plate into the metaphysis and diaphysis, representing islands of chondroid tissue that failed to ossify. The combination with platyspondyly gave the disorder its name in 1976.

evidence.snippet: All patients exhibited short stature and skeletal abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Cohort frequency for short stature.

evidence.snippet: skeletal disease, manifest as short stature and/or leg pain/bowing, was the reason for initial presentation in 12 patients (46%), with height varying between the normal range to 6.5 SD below the mean
evidence.explanation: Supports the FREQUENT rather than VERY_FREQUENT band, since height can be normal.

steps/12.description: Short stature is common but not obligate; height spans the normal range to 6.5 standard deviations below the mean, and some patients have minimal or no skeletal manifestations in early childhood.

evidence.snippet: All our patients had spasticity with variable associations of motor and mental delay or epilepsy. All except for one patient had bilateral calcification in the basal ganglia.
evidence.explanation: Documents spasticity in all patients of the series.

evidence.snippet: observed spasticity in 11 patients (44%), and intracranial calcification on computed tomography imaging in 9 of 13 patients assessed
evidence.explanation: Gives the 44 percent frequency behind the FREQUENT band.

steps/13.description: Increased tone, sometimes clinically evident within the first months of life, recorded in 44 percent of one genetically defined cohort.

evidence.snippet: All our patients had spasticity with variable associations of motor and mental delay or epilepsy. All except for one patient had bilateral calcification in the basal ganglia.
evidence.explanation: Documents basal ganglia calcification in nearly all patients of the series.

evidence.snippet: intracranial calcification on computed tomography imaging in 9 of 13 patients assessed, variably involving the basal ganglia, pons, cerebellar dentate nuclei, and white-grey matter junction
evidence.explanation: Nine of thirteen assessed patients supports the VERY_FREQUENT band among those imaged.

steps/14.description: Calcification on computed tomography, variably involving the basal ganglia, pons, cerebellar dentate nuclei, and the grey-white matter junction; present in 9 of 13 assessed patients and detectable in early infancy.

evidence.snippet: Spondyloenchondrodysplasia (SPENCD) is an immune-osseous disorder caused by biallelic variants in ACP5 gene and is less commonly associated with neurological abnormalities such as global developmental delay, spasticity and seizures.
evidence.explanation: Names global developmental delay among the neurological features.
